problems.title: Polar winter in Antarctic
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Polar winter in Antarctic

Nitric acid hydrates have received much attention as possible catalysts for heterogeneous reactions that bring about the Antarctic ozone hole. Worsnop et al. has measured thermodynamic parameters for sublimation of nitric acid mono-, di- and trihydrates at 220 K:

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} & \Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ,\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} & \Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ,\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{HNO3*H2O(s) -> HNO3(g) + H2O(g)} & 46.2 & 127 \\ \hline \ce{HNO3*2H2O(s) -> HNO3(g) + 2H2O(g)} & 69.4 & 188 \\ \hline \ce{HNO3*3H2O(s) -> HNO3(g) + 3H2O(g)} & 93.2 & 237 \end{array}$$

a) Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ$ at 190 K (the conditions of the polar winter stratosphere). Assume that $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ$ do not depend on temperature.

a) Which hydrate is thermodynamically most stable at 190 K if $p(\ce{H2O}) = 1.3\cdot10^{-7}$ bar and $p(\ce{HNO3}) = 4.1\cdot10^{-10}$ bar? Standard pressure is 1 bar.

problems.title: Synthesis of bicyclic compound
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Synthesis of bicyclic compound

The bicyclic skeleton of compound $\mathbf{X}$ appears in many naturally occurring alkaloids. The simple approach to the synthesis of title compound is outlined in this problem. At the heart of the synthesis is a nitro-aldol reaction between benzaldehyde and nitromethane.

a) Explain, why nitromethane is acidic enough for an aldol reaction to occur?

b) Under basic reaction conditions benzaldehyde and nitromethane in nitro-aldol reaction give compound $\mathbf{A}$ (molecular formula $\ce{C8H7NO2}$). Based on the knowledge of the classical aldol reaction suggest structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-2-fig1.png

c) $\mathbf{A}$ is fully reduced with hydrogen using palladium on charcoal as a catalyst to give $\mathbf{B}$ (molecular formula $\ce{C8H11N}$). $\mathbf{B}$ is fairly basic and readily forms salts with acids. Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{B}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-2-fig2.png

d) $\mathbf{B}$ under acidic reaction conditions reacts with formaldehyde to give final compound $\mathbf{X}$. This transformation proceeds through formation of $\mathbf{C}$ (molecular formula $\ce{C9H11N}$), which under these reaction conditions undergoes cyclization to form bicyclic $\mathbf{X}$ (molecular formula $\ce{C9H11N}$). $\mathbf{X}$ is fairly basic and is usually isolated in a form of salt. Using your knowledge of reactivity of carbonyl compounds suggest structures of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-2-fig3.png

problems.title: Isoleucine dating
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Isoleucine dating

The rate of isomerization of isoleucine in fossilized bone can be used as an indication of the average temperature of the sample storage.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-3-fig1.png

At 20°C this reaction has a half-life of 125000 years and its activation energy is 139.7 kJ/mol. After a very long time, the ratio allo/iso reaches an equilibrium value of 1.38. You may assume that this equilibrium constant does not depend on temperature.

The time dependence of concentration for a reversible reaction is given by equation:

$$\ln\left(\frac{[\mathrm{A}]-[\mathrm{A}]_\mathrm{eq}}{[\mathrm{A}]_0-[\mathrm{A}]_\mathrm{eq}}\right) = -\left(k_1+k_{-1}\right)t$$

For a hippopotamus mandible which lived near a warm spring in South Africa, the present allo/iso ratio in bones is 0.42. Radiocarbon dating, which is temperature independent, determined the age of hippo tooth, which was 38600 years.

a) Assuming that no allo was present initially, determine constants for forward and reverse reactions and overall isomerization constant ($k_1 + k_{-1}$).

b) Calculate an average conservation temperature of the hippopotamus remains in soil.

problems.title: Goblin’s element
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Goblin’s element

Metal $\mathbf{X}$ was discovered in 1735. Its name has derived from a German word meaning “goblin” or “evil spirit”.

A sample of metal $\mathbf{X}$ immersed in $\ce{H2O}$ weights 13.031 g. Meanwhile the weight of the same sample in $\ce{CCl4}$ is 12.046 g. The density of $\ce{CCl4}$ is $1.5940\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

In order to identify the metal $\mathbf{X}$, neutron diffraction is used. The diffraction pattern is specific to the FCC structure and the angle of the reflection ($2\theta$) from the (222) plane is 76.956°. The velocity of neutrons in the diffractometer is 3115.0 m/s.

The same sample is heated in $\ce{O2}$ atmosphere until metal X has reacted completely. The product of the reaction is compound $\mathbf{A}$ containing 26.577% of oxygen (by mass). All the amount of compound $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with diluted HCl releasing 1.0298 L of $\ce{O2}$ at 25.00ºC temperature and 100.0 kPa pressure, giving salt $\mathbf{B}$ and water only.

Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is dissolved in an aqueous solution containing $\ce{Cl^-}$, $\ce{Br^-}$ and $\ce{I^-}$ ions. Complex ion $\mathbf{C}$ forms as one of the products. The formula of ion $\mathbf{C}$ is $[\ce{XCl2Br2I2}]^{n-}$ and it is a paramagnetic.

Complex carbonyl compound $\mathbf{D}$ is prepared by heating metal $\mathbf{X}$ under a high pressure of carbon monoxide. The formula of compound $\mathbf{D}$ is $[\mathbf{X}_2\ce{(CO)8}]$ and it is a diamagnetic. The both atoms of metal $\mathbf{X}$ are equivalent in the structure of compound $\mathbf{D}$. A CO molecule donates a pair of electrons to form a single bond only but not all the CO molecules are equivalent in the structure of compound $\mathbf{D}$.

a) Calculate the density of metal $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

b) Calculate the unit cell parameter ($a$) of metal $\mathbf{X}$ in pm.

c) Calculate the molar mass of metal $\mathbf{X}$ in g/mol. What element is metal $\mathbf{X}$?

d) Write a chemical formula of compound $\mathbf{A}$.

e) Write a balanced chemical equation of the reaction of compound $\mathbf{A}$ with diluted HCl.

f) Sketch the spatial structures of all possible isomers (including structural, geometrical and optical) of ion $\mathbf{C}$.

g) Count the number of unpaired electrons in ion $\mathbf{C}$. Consider halogenides as weak field ligands

h) Sketch the spatial structure of compound $\mathbf{D}$.

problems.title: Sigmatropic rearrangement
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Sigmatropic rearrangement

Pericyclic reactions are concerted processes that occur by way of a cyclic transition state in which more than one bond is formed or broken within the cycle. The so called sigmatropic rearrangements constitute a large group of pericyclic reactions. Of all the sigmatropic rearrangements, the [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement has been used most in organic synthesis. The reaction involves the transformation of 1,5-dienes and all-carbon system is known as the Cope rearrangement, whereas with an allyl vinyl ether the reaction is termed a Claisen rearrangement. The examples of these reactions are given bellow:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-5-fig1.png

The sigmatropic rearrangement has been use in many syntheses of the complex molecules and has industrial applications as well.

1. The key step in the synthesis of the alkaloid strychnine was made by use of this chemistry:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-5-fig2.png

2. The chemical company BASF manufactures citral (intermediate in the synthesis of vitamin A) by the remarkable synthesis shown bellow:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2007-5-fig3.png

Write the reaction mechanism (except for the loss of water in the example 2) and possible intermediates for both reactions.

HINT: by treating acetaldehyde with ethanol under the same reaction conditions as in example 2, vinylethyl ether could be obtained.

problems.title: Dolomite
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Dolomite

One of the most widespread minerals is dolomite, which in huge amounts is also in bowels of the earth of Baltic States. Dolomite contains two metallic elements $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. Metal $\mathbf{A}$ crystallizes in hexagonal close packed atomic structure (unit cell parameters: $a = 3.2094$ Å, $b = 3.2094$ Å, $c = 5.2108$ Å and $\gamma = 120^\mathrm{o}$), while metal $\mathbf{B}$ crystallizes in cubic close packed atomic structure (unit cell parameter: $a = 5.5884$ Å).

a) What are metals $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$? Calculate atomic radii for these elements!

b) Calculate by how many percent (of initial atomic radii) reduce radii for both metallic elements, when ions are produced from atoms. It is known that oxides of both elements have sodium chloride structure and radii of oxide anion is 1.28 Å. Unit cell parameters for both oxides are 4.213 Å un 4.811 Å, respectively.

Industrially metal $\mathbf{A}$ can be produced from sea water. To purify chloride of metal $\mathbf{A}$ from other salts hydroxide of metal $\mathbf{B}$ is added to sea water. The obtained white precipitate is dissolved in hydrochloric acid and evaporated, till metal $\mathbf{A}$ salt hydrate forms. Then the hydrate is heated and salt melted and electrolyzed.

c) Write down equations of all chemical reactions described above and calculate time for electrolysis which has to be performed to isolate 1.0 ton of metal $\mathbf{A}$. Current intensity 9.0 kA.

One of the most favorite reactions for students is burning of metal $\mathbf{A}$ in the air. Reaction produces huge amount of UV light and two binary compounds, one of them is oxide of metal $\mathbf{A}$.

d) What is the second compound that is produced in this reaction? Write equations of both reactions and propose chemical reactions which could be useful for experimental identification of this compound.

Metal $\mathbf{A}$ also is used in army of USA, for preparing food in field conditions. To heat food wrapped in aluminum foil a special heater (in English Flameless Ration Heater), which contains 30 mL water, is used. Heating material is a composite, where powder of metal $\mathbf{A}$ and iron are associated in matrix of high density polyethylene. In presence of chloride ions metal $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with water, forming hydroxide and hydrogen, which is available for burning to obtain extra heat.

e) Using thermodynamical constants shown below calculate minimal mass of element $\mathbf{A}$, which is needed for heating 1.0 L of water from temperature 20°C to 100°C. Assume that all chemical reactions proceed under standard conditions.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \text{Compound} & \Delta H_\mathrm{f,298}\ (\mathrm{kJ/mol}) & C_\mathrm{p}\ (\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}) \\ \hline \ce{H2},\ g & 0 & 28{,}83 \\ \hline \ce{H2O},\ g & -241{,}81 & 33{,}61 \\ \hline \ce{H2O},\ l & -285{,}83 & 75{,}30 \\ \hline \text{Metal } \mathbf{A},\ s & 0 & 24{,}89 \\ \hline \text{Hydroxide of metal } \mathbf{A},\ s & -924{,}66 & 76{,}99 \end{array}$$

f) Metal $\mathbf{A}$ hydroxide, which forms in reaction, is slightly soluble. Calculate solubility (mg/L; milligrams per liter) of mentioned hydroxide in distilled water. $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{s} = 11{,}25$.

problems.title: Hydrolysis of pyrophosphate
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Hydrolysis of pyrophosphate (10 pts)

Let’s take a look at the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate ($\ce{P2O7^{4-}}$) by the enzyme. It is assumed that the concentration of pyrophosphate is much lower than the Michaelis constant; thus, the reaction is formally supposed to be first-order. At pH = 7 at 25 °C the apparent first-order rate constant is $k_7^* = 0{,}0010\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The mechanism of the hydrolysis is as follows:

$$\ce{H2P2O7^{2-} <=> HP2O7^{3-} <=> P2O7^{4-} -> 2HPO4^{2-}}$$

where $\mathrm{p}K_1 = 6.12$ ja $\mathrm{p}K_2 = 8.95$ are the acid dissociation constants (1st and 2nd stages), and $k$ is the true rate constant which does not depend on pH (3rd stage). It is assumed that acid dissociations are fast compared with the hydrolysis.

a) Write down the equations for the acid dissociation constants $K_1$ and $K_2$, and derive an expression of pyrophosphate total concentration.

b) Calculate the value of true rate constant $k$.

c) Calculate the values of apparent rate constants $k_6^*$ and $k_8^*$ at pH = 6 and pH = 8.

problems.title: Iodine and polyiodides
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Iodine and polyiodides (12 pts)

Iodine was discovered in 1811 by the French chemist Curtois during the process of manufacturing potassium nitrate, with which he supplied the Napoleon armies. While washing seaweed ashes with sulphuric acid, he noticed violet fumes that condensed on his copper equipment and caused corrosion. Below you see diagram that represents some iodine chemistry. Only iodine containing substances $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{H}$ are indicated in this diagram. In some cases it might be more reaction products.

a) Identify substances $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{H}$ and write appropriate balanced molecular chemical equations:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-2-fig1.png

One of remarkable features of iodine is possibility to form so called polyiodide ions. One of the simplest polyiodide ion present in tincture of iodine. This tincture is prepared by dissolution of iodine $\ce{I2}$ in a solution of $\ce{KI}$. In this mixture triiodide ions $\ce{I3^-}$ present. Until now anions from $\ce{I2^-}$ to $\ce{I29^{3-}}$ have been established.

b) Write Lewis structure for $\ce{I3^-}$ ion. Don’t forget to indicate lone pairs of electrons. Show geometrical arrangement of iodine atoms in this ion.

c) Draw possible geometrical structures of $\ce{I5^-}$ ion. In this case you might omit lone pairs of electrons.

Polyiodides are not very stable compounds, but large cations with a high symmetry can be used to obtain thermally stable polyiodides. In the laboratory polyiodide $\mathrm{R_4NI}_{2x+1}$ ($x$ = 1, 2, 3, 4 ...) with large cation was investigated. R is radical of alkane. For titration of 0.219 g of $\mathrm{R_4NI}_{2x+1}$ 10.23 mL of 0.112 mol/L $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution was consumed. In the course of titration $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ is converted into $\ce{S4O6^{2-}}$.

d) Determine molecular formula of $\mathrm{R_4NI}_{2x+1}$. Clearly show your calculations.

problems.title: Small rings fighting diabetes
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Small rings fighting diabetes (10 pts)

The scheme shown below represents the industrial synthesis of a new class of drugs for treatment of type 2 diabetes. The synthesis, remarkable in its simplicity and especially in effortless purification of products, is used to produce the target molecule in kilogram quantities for clinical development.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-3-fig1.png

1. Provide structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$. ($\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ are 2 pt each; $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ are 1 pt each)

2. Suggest the mechanism for the formation of $\mathbf{D}$ from $\mathbf{C}$. Consider this reaction as a three step process. Formation of the active reagent from sulfur compound and strong base, its addition to $\mathbf{C}$ and elimination of side product to give $\mathbf{D}$. (1 pt for each step, 3 pts total)

problems.title: Uses and misuses of nitrogen compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Uses and misuses of nitrogen compounds (10 pts)

The thermal decomposition of urea at 175 °C affords the highly symmetrical, acidic ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 7$) compound $\mathbf{A}$ (composition: C 27,9%, H 2,3%, N 32,6%, O 37,2%) along with colorless gas $\mathbf{B}$. Compound $\mathbf{A}$ exists in solution as a mixture of isomers $\mathbf{A1}$ and $\mathbf{A2}$, where aromatic isomer $\mathbf{A1}$ is the predominant form.

$\mathbf{A}$ can be converted into two different chlorides $\mathbf{C1}$ (N 22,8%) and $\mathbf{C2}$ (N 18,1%). $\mathbf{C1}$ is well suited for multiple functionalizations with nucleophiles and is commonly used as a precursor in production of pesticides and fluorescent dyes, while $\mathbf{C2}$ found its widespread use as water disinfectant and bleaching agent.

Although it is not commercially viable, compound $\mathbf{D}$, in principle, could be obtained from $\mathbf{C1}$ and gas $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{D}$ has very high nitrogen content (66,6%). The use of $\mathbf{D}$ in dairy products to artificially boost protein content was at the core of the scandal in China in 2008.

$\mathbf{C1}$ is also widely utilized in organic synthesis. The wide range of reagents based on $\mathbf{C1}$ allows simple one step transformation of a carboxylic acid into amide, ester and even into alcohol. Sequentially treating $\mathbf{C1}$ with methanol then N-methylpiperidine (NMP) affords coupling agent $\mathbf{E}$ (N 20,4%) in a form of the chloride salt.

Coupling reagent $\mathbf{E}$ is primarily used in the synthesis of various amides. Although $\mathbf{E}$ is cheap and easy to use, which allows the synthesis even on multikilogram scale, it has one significant drawback. The reaction solvent choice is limited to tetrahydrofuran. In other solvents, like chloroform or acetonitrile, $\mathbf{E}$ undergoes rapid degradation with formation of neutral compound $\mathbf{F}$ (N 25,0%) and gas $\mathbf{G}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-4-fig1.png

1. Provide structures of compounds $\mathbf{A1}$, $\mathbf{A2}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C1}$, $\mathbf{C2}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$. (1 pt each, $\mathbf{B}$ is 0,5 pt)

2. Suggest simple solution to avoid degradation of activating agent $\mathbf{E}$. (0,75 pt)

3. Draw the mechanism of conversion of carboxylic acid $\ce{RCOOH}$ into amide $\ce{RCONHR'}$, using activating agent $\mathbf{E}$. (0,75 pt)

problems.title: Kinetics and equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Kinetics and equilibrium (8 pts)

Under standard condition the rate constant for the reaction $\ce{CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3}$ is $0.0375\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and under normal condition — $0.0021\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Under standard condition $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0 = 4730\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^0 = -33{,}5\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$. Assume that $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^0$ under normal condition have the same values.

a) Calculate the equilibrium constants of the reaction at 0 °C and 25 °C.

b) Calculate the activation energy for the backward reaction.

problems.title: Chanel №5
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Chanel №5 (10 pts)

The legendary fragnance Chanel No. 5 was created in 1921 and retains it’s popularity nowadays. It was the favorite Marilyn Monroe’s perfume. She noted she only slept wearing a few drops of Chanel No. 5. One of the stories tell that this scent was accidentally made by the assistant adding too much of 2-methylundecanal to the mixture.

Like the majority of all the perfumes’ components, 2-methylundecanal is a purely synthetic artificial substance, so a convenient synthesis was proposed. $\ce{^{13}C}$ carbon isotope was used to make the investigation on the reaction mechanism easier.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-6-fig1.png

a) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

b) Write down the mechanisms of the first and the third reaction.

A stereoselective synthesis of (R)-2-methylundecanal $\mathbf{G}$ was suggested also to find out which one of the two enantiomers has the required odour for the perfume. The asymmetric center was introduced using a chiral 2-(methoxymethyl)-pyrrolidin-1-amine $\mathbf{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-6-fig2.png

c) Draw the structure of (R)-2-methylundecanal $\mathbf{G}$.

d) Which 2-(methoxymethyl)pyrrolidin-1-amine $\mathbf{C}$ enantiomer is used in the synthesis? Why?

e) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{D}$ – $\mathbf{F}$.

After completing the synthesis it was discovered that both the isomers have very similar smells.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2009-6-fig3.png

problems.title: Ethanol as sourse of energy
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Ethanol as sourse of energy (10 points)

Since ancient times ethanol has been used for lamp oil and cooking, along with plant and animal oils. Nowadays vast majority of ethanol is used as fuel and is produced in large scale by fermentation, in which certain species of yeast metabolize sugar producing ethanol. It can be said that sunlight is used to run the engine of a vehicles, as a simple sugar is created in the plant by photosynthesis, and during ethanol combustion carbon dioxide and water are produced with a release of energy.

a) Write chemical equations for sugar synthesis, ethanol production and combustion.

Early in 1860 Nikolaus August Otto used ethyl alcohol as a fuel in internal combustion engine. Today ethanol may be used as a fuel to power both direct-ethanol fuel cells (DEFC) and combustion engines. One of the first DEFC, which schematic diagram is given, was introduced in the ShellEco-Marathon in 2007.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-1-fig1.png

b) Identify chemical species $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{F}$ on figure.

c) From thermodynamic data calculate DEFC maximal energy conversion efficiency ratio: $\eta = \Delta_\mathrm{r}G^0/\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0$ (25 °C).$^1$

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{compound} & \ce{O2} & \ce{H2} & \ce{CO2} & \ce{H2O} & \ce{C2H5OH} & \ce{C6H12O6} \\ \hline \Delta H^0,\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 0 & 0 & -394 & -286 & -278 & -1273 \\ \hline S^0,\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 205 & 131 & 214 & 70 & 161 & 212 \end{array}$$

$^1$ Give all the ansvers with two signifant numbers.

d) For comparison calculate efficiency of combustion engine running on Otto cycle using equation for maximal efficiency: $\eta = 1 - 1/r^{(\gamma-1)}$, where $\gamma = C_\mathrm{p}/C_\mathrm{V} \approx 1.4$, $r$ is compression ratio which equals 9 and 12.5 for ethanol and gasoline, respectively. Assume, that only half of the efficiency is achieved in practice.

There are several unsolved issues concerning DEFC, thus, in closer perspective it is more promising to convert ethanol into hydrogen in order to use the latter in typical hydrogen fuel cell.

e) Using given data calculate the maximal energy conversion efficiency ratio ($\eta = \Delta_\mathrm{r}G^0/\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0$) of the hydrogen fuel cell.

To be realistic, it should be considered that in order to move a vehicle the electric energy must be converted into mechanical. Let's assume that conversion efficiency of subsystems are: 90% for invertor, 90% for motor, and 90% for gas compressor. Overall conversion efficiency ratio may be compared to energy conversion efficiency ratio of combustion engine in which chemical energy is directly converted to mechanical.

f) Estimate overall efficiency of hydrogen vehicle.

g) Name one-two main advantages of i) ethanol over gasoline fuel in internal combustion engine; ii) fuel cell over internal combustion engine.

problems.title: Synthesis and Aquation of Fluoropentaaquachromium(III) ion
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Synthesis and Aquation of Fluoropentaaquachromium(III) ion$^2$ (10 points)

$5.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ 2.0 M chromium(III) perchlorate and $5.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ 2.0 M potassium fluoride were brougt together; the solution was boiled under reflux for 3 hours and cooled to 0 °C, and the precipitate $\mathbf{X}$ was removed. The density of all solutions is $1.1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

a) In the water solution the chromium(III) perchlorate is presented as aquachromium cation with co-ordination number equal to six. Write the formula of aquachromium cation and the precipitate $\mathbf{X}$.

b) During the reflux the water in the inner sphere of the complex is replaced by anion. Write the equation of reaction.

c) The solubility product of the salt $\mathbf{X}$ is $K_\mathrm{sp} = 2.9\cdot10^{-3}$ at 0 °C, but it is possible to dissolve 10.9 g of the salt in $5\underline{0}$ g water at 100 °C ($\rho = 1.1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$). Calculate how many grams of salt $\mathbf{X}$ did precipitate during the cooling process.

$^2$ The problem is based on T.W. Swaddle, E.L. King Inorg. Chem. 4 (1965) 532.

d) The reaction mixture contained various complexes of chromium. Cation-exchange (contains $\ce{R-SO3H}$ groups) separation allowed isolation of hexaaquachromium(III) ions, fluoropentaaquachromium(III) ions, difluorotetraaquachromium(III) ions and hydrolytic dimers of chromium. During the eluation process the sample was first taken into the column and afterwards the ions were eluated out using $\ce{HClO4}$ with varing concentration. Identify to which species the peaks correspond on the chromatogram.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-2-fig1.png

Which compound would come out of the column during the process of taking the sample into the column?

The contents of chromium and fluoride in purified fluoropentaaquachromium(III) ions was established. $10.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the sample was first decomposed using the alkaline solution of hydrogen peroxide. The fluoride ion is liberated and the oxydation state of chromium changes from III to VI. After that the sample was divided into two equal parts. First part was acidified using conc. $\ce{HCl}$ and then 3 g $\ce{KI}$ was added. After standing 5 min the solution was titrated using $18.5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ 0.0975 M $\ce{Na2S2O3}$. The endpoint was determined using starch solution. The second part was analysed using the fluoride ion selective electrode which was calibrated using solutions with known concentration of $\ce{F-}$. The equation of calibration curve was $E = 183\,\mathrm{mV} - 56\,\mathrm{mV}\cdot\log\left[\ce{F-}\right]$. The reading of the voltmeter was 252.6 mV and the final volume of the solution was $1\underline{0}\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ after adjusting the pH of the solution to six.

e) Write all the equations of chemial reactions in the analysis process and calculate the ration of $n(\mathrm{F})/n(\mathrm{Cr})$ in the sample.

The pseudo first order rate coefficient of aquation of fluoropentaaquachromium(III) ion

$$\ce{[Cr(H2O)5F]^{2+} + H+ + H2O = [Cr(H2O)6]^{3+} + HF}\quad(\mathbf{I})$$

is

$$k = \frac{2.303\left(\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_0 - \left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_\infty\right)}{t\left(\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_0 + \left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_\infty\right)}\log\frac{\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_0^2 - \left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]\,\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_\infty}{\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_0\left(\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right] - \left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_\infty\right)}$$

where $\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_0 = 5.28\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ is the starting concentration and $\left[\ce{CrF^{2+}}\right]_\infty$ equilibrium concentration of the complex ion.

f) Calculate the time $t$ (h) needed to aquate $7\underline{0}\%$ of the complex ion at 77.2 °C if the concentration of hydrogen ions is 0.414 M, the rate constant is $4.40\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and equilibrium constant of the reaction is 0.048. The water is in excess and not included in the equilibrium constant.

The hydrofluoric acid is weak acid.

g) Calculate $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\ce{HF})$ at 25ºC if the equilibrium constant of the

$$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^{3+} + F- = [Cr(H2O)5F]^{2+} + H2O}\quad(\mathbf{II})$$

reaction is $K = 2.1\cdot10^{4}$ (25 °C) and for the reaction ($\mathbf{I}$) the reaction enthalpy is $-5.41\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

problems.title: Asymmetry without asymmetric center
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Asymmetry without asymmetric center (10 points)

Allenes are not only versatile starting materials in organic synthesis but also present an interesting case of molecular chirality. Since it is quite difficult to synthesize allenes in stereoselective manner, they are first obtained as racemic mixture and then resolved into individual enantiomers. One of the ways of synthesizing allenes in depicted below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-3-fig1.png

a) Identify symmetric structure $\mathbf{A}$. Keep in mind that this reaction is not very efficient and $\mathbf{A}$ is only one of few possible products in this reaction.

b) Provide the mechanism for conversion of $\mathbf{A}$ into an allene.

One of the methods to produce allenes in pure enantiomeric form is dynamic resolution of racemic mixtures. The method takes advantage of quick epimerization and the low solubility of one of the stereoisomers. Epimerization means interconversion of one enantiomer into another proceeding through a common intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ (see scheme below). Since all of the compounds are in the equilibrium, the position of the equilibrium is shifted in the direction of the less soluble stereoisomer, which is then collected as a precipitate.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-3-fig2.png

Reaction conditions: room temperature, $\ce{Et3N}$ (0.05 Eq), pentane; R* is (-)-menthyl

c) Provide the structure of $\mathbf{B}$.

In order to establish the absolute configuration of the allene $\mathbf{X}$ obtained by dynamic resolution, one can follow a method developed by Agosta in 1964. To better understand the essence of the method let us consider all transformations performed on BOTH enantiomers.

The allene ester is first hydrolyzed to dicarboxylic acid and then in Diels-Alder reaction with cyclopentadiene is transformed into a mixure of separable products.

$$\mathrm{R^{*}O_2CHC{=}C{=}CHCO_2R^{*}} \xrightarrow{\text{a)}} \underset{\text{Single enantiomer}}{\mathrm{HO_2CHC{=}C{=}CHCO_2H}} \xrightarrow{\text{b)}} \mathbf{C}_{1\text{-}4}$$

a) $\ce{NaOH}$; b) cyclopentadiene

d) Provide structures for ALL possible adducts with cyclopentadiene that could be formed from EACH allene enatiomer ($\mathbf{C}_{1\text{-}4}$ from one allene enantiomer, and $\mathbf{C}_{5\text{-}8}$ from the other). You are allowed to use molecular models provided by organizers.

[In the answer space, the left structure below heads the column for $\mathbf{C}_{1\text{-}4}$ and the right structure the column for $\mathbf{C}_{5\text{-}8}$:]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-3-fig3.png

Each of the individual compounds $\mathrm{C}_{1\text{-}8}$ is then subjected to 2 test reactions: a) iodolactonization and b) cyclic anhydride formation.

$$\mathbf{D} \xleftarrow{\text{a)}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\text{b)}} \mathbf{E}$$

a) $\ce{I2}$, $\ce{NaHCO3}$; b) acetic anhydride

e) In your list of adducts, identify which structures $\mathbf{C}_{1\text{-}8}$ are capable of giving desired products in BOTH test reactions. Draw equation for ONE iodolactonization reaction ($\mathbf{D}$) and ONE cyclic anhydride formation ($\mathbf{E}$).

The compound(s) $\mathbf{C}$ that gives positive result in both test reactions is (are) then degraded according to the following scheme. The product of the reaction $\mathbf{F}$ ($\ce{C7H10O}$) is optically active compound.

$$\mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\text{a)-d)}} \mathbf{F}\quad \ce{C7H10O}$$

a) Pd/C, $\ce{H2}$; b) $\ce{CH2N2}$; c) $\ce{O3}$; d) $\ce{HCl}$, reflux

In summary, the explicit assignment of the absolute configuration by method of Agosta is based on the fact that one enantiomer of $\mathbf{F}$ can only be produced from (R)-allene, while the opposite enantiomer of $\mathbf{F}$ stems only from the (S)-allene.

f) In aforementioned case of dynamic resolution of allenes the degradation yields exclusively (1S,4R)-$\mathbf{F}$ stereoisomer. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{F}$.

g) Based on the structure of compound (1S,4R)-F and identification method by Agosta suggest the structure of allene $\mathbf{X}$, which was obtained by dynamic resolution.

problems.title: Environmental hazards
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Environmental hazards (10 points)

Around World War II Jinzu River in Toyama prefecture Japan was contaminated with element $\mathbf{X_1}$ compounds and nowadays Japan still is one of top three producers of this element. Element $\mathbf{X_1}$ accumulates in rice and can cause Itai-Itai disease in humans; it also replaces calcium in bones. This element is produced from compound $\mathbf{A}$ which is its only mineral of practical importance. Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is also a direct band gap semiconductor and has many applications for example in light detectors and as thermally stable pigments.

Binary compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains also nonmetallic element $\mathbf{Y_1}$ and this compound forms minerals greenockite (first discovered in Scotland and named after the land owner Lord Greenock) and hawleyite. The first mineral has hexagonal structure while second mineral has cubic structure. Mass fraction of $\mathbf{X_1}$ in compound $\mathbf{A}$ is 77.6%.

Element $\mathbf{X_1}$ can be obtained from $\mathbf{A}$ by roasting it in air. Obtained oxide is treated with sulfur trioxide to form $\mathbf{X_1}$ sulfate which is dissolved in water and electrolyzed.

a) Determine element $\mathbf{X_1}$, show your calculations!

b) Write equations for all mentioned reactions taking place in element production!

c) Calculate mass of metal $\mathbf{X_1}$ which can be obtained by electrolysis of 0.15 M metal sulfate solution with 0.5 A current and one hour long.

d) Write electron formula for element $\mathbf{X_1}$ ions in sulfate solution, knowing that there are no f electrons in this ion.

e) Table with lattice parameters for greenockite and hawleyite is shown bellow. Calculate $Z$ value (number of “molecules” in unit cell) for hawleyite as well as density for greenockite.

Cell parameters of minerals are given below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Parameter} & \text{Greenockite} & \text{Hawleyite} \\ \hline \text{System} & \text{hexagonal} & \text{cubic} \\ \text{Parameters} & \begin{array}{c} a = b = 3.82\ \text{Å} \\ c = 6.26\ \text{Å} \\ \gamma = 120^\mathrm{o}\ \text{(angle between } a \\ \text{and } b\text{)} \end{array} & a = 5.818\ \text{Å} \\ Z & 2 & ? \\ \text{Density} & ? & 4.87\ \mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}} \end{array}$$

Practically important is also compound $\mathbf{B}$ which is used for production of solar energy panels and which contains nonmetallic element $\mathbf{Y_2}$. Mass fraction of element $\mathbf{X_1}$ in compound $\mathbf{B}$ is less than 50% and it is known that element $\mathbf{Y_2}$ is in same group as element $\mathbf{Y_1}$ but electronegativity for element $\mathbf{Y_2}$ is smaller than for $\mathbf{Y_1}$.

f) Determine element $\mathbf{Y_2}$, show your calculations!

Usually element $\mathbf{X_1}$ is found together with element $\mathbf{X_2}$ which is placed in same group in periodic table. Binary compound of element $\mathbf{X_2}$ with $\mathbf{Y_1}$ crystallizes in cubic face centered crystals (FCC) with parameter $a = 5.406$ Å. Density of this compound is $4.09\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

g) Determine element $\mathbf{X_2}$, show your calculations!

h) Order all possible binary compounds from elements $\mathbf{X_1}$, $\mathbf{X_2}$, $\mathbf{Y_1}$ and $\mathbf{Y_2}$ in order of increasing covalent bond content and decreasing ionic bond content!

Elements $\mathbf{X_1}$ and $\mathbf{X_2}$ can be separated also due to different solubilities of their hydroxides. Hydroxides and carbonates are the forms of $\mathbf{X_1}$ compounds which are now found in Jinzu River bed ($\mathbf{X_1}$ concentration aprox. 2 ppm).

i) Which element ($\mathbf{X_1}$ or $\mathbf{X_2}$) hydroxide has better solubility in alkaline solutions? Explain it with atomic structure of elements.

It is possible to answer next question without answering previous ones!

j) Calculate solubility (express in mol/L) of both compounds in water pH = 10.0! Take into account complex ion formation! All necessary data are given in table In the table logarithms of the overall formation constants are given.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{II} \\ \hline \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{sp}\ \text{of hydroxide} & 14.14 & 16.5 \\ \mathrm{p}K_1 & 4.17 & 4.40 \\ \mathrm{p}K_{1,2} & 8.33 & 11.30 \\ \mathrm{p}K_{1,2,3} & 9.02 & 14.14 \\ \mathrm{p}K_{1,2,3,4} & 8.62 & 17.66 \end{array}$$

problems.title: Half solid half melted
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Half solid half melted (10 points)

In 1914, Tubandt and Lorenz showed that solid silver iodide above 147 °C transforms into $\alpha$-AgI modification that is good electrical conductor. Temperature of 147 °C may be considered as melting point for silver ion sublattice. The remaining iodide ion sublattice is stable until 557 °C. It was determined that iodide ions form body centered cubic (BCC) sublattice with lattice constant (lattice parameter) $5.04\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$.

In picture the principal scheme of Tuband’s electrochemical cell is shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-5-fig1.png

In this cell silver electrodes 0.1000 g each were placed in contact with both sides of solid $\ce{AgI}$ pellet Then electric current of 35.2 mA was flowed for 15.5 min. After that silver electrodes where taken off the pellet and were placed into two labelled $100.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flasks (label “Solution A” for anode and “Solution B” for cathode). Excess of diluted $\ce{HNO3(aq)}$ was added into both flasks. After dissolution of metallic electrodes both volumetric flasks were filled with distilled water till calibration mark. Solution A and Solution B were used for titration of $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ samples of $0.0113\,\mathrm{mol\cdot dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{NaCl}$ solution that contains small amount of $\ce{K2CrO4}$. Endpoint for these titrations were appearance of brick-red precipitate.

a) Write half-reactions that represent what was happening at the anode and at the cathode during the electric current flow.

b) Write balanced chemical equation that is proceeding during action of diluted nitric acid $\ce{HNO3(aq)}$ onto electrodes.

c) Write formula of the brick-red compound that precipitates at the titration endpoint.

d) Calculate the ratio V(Solution A)/V(Solution B) (ratio of volumes of respectively solutions that were used up for the titration of samples of $\ce{NaCl}$ solution).

e) Determine radius of iodide ion in BCC sublattice.

f) Calculate density of solid $\ce{AgI}$ conductor.

g) $\ce{AgI}$ is light sensitive compound suitable for photography. After development of black-white photo the image should be “fixed” by dissolving away all remaining silver iodide (or other silver salts). Sodium thiosulfate $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ is suitable fixing agent. Under reaction with silver iodide it produces compound that contains 26.9% of silver by mass. Write chemical equation that shows what is happening during the “fixing” black-white photo.

problems.title: Modafinil – work without sleep ?
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Modafinil – work without sleep ? (10 points)

Modafinil was originally created to treat narcolepsy (a condition when a person falls asleep at inappropriate times), but it spread widely among students and businessmen. Although a productive day after a sleepless night sounds unbelievable, it is not the only effect of modafinil; it also acts as an antidepressant and improves memory in some cases. Modafinil has a considerably smaller list of side effects than caffeine but due to its unknown long-term effects it remains a prescription drug. Yet this doesn’t scare most of its users off, who buy it from the internet shops or illegal dealers.

An industrial synthesis scheme of Modafinil is presented below. In the $^1$H NMR spectrum of compound $\mathbf{A}$ there is one singlet (6.0 ppm) and ten times more intensive multiplet (7.3 ppm). In its mass spectrum two peaks of equal intensity for the molecular ion are observed at 246 and 248 m/z. After treating compound $\mathbf{A}$ with sodium hydrosulfide a side product $\mathbf{C}'$ was detected, therefore to avoid its formation one additional step was introduced in the synthesis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2010-6-fig1.png

a) Draw the structural formulas of all letter-named compounds.

b) Present the mechanism for the reaction $\mathbf{D} \rightarrow \mathbf{E}$.

Modafinil is actually a mixture of two enantiomers, where only the R isomer shows the indicated biological activity.

c) Draw the structural formula of the active enantiomer of Modafinil.

problems.title: Aluminium
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Aluminium (6 points)

Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth‘s crust. Some compounds of aluminium, like alum (the double sulphate $\ce{KAl(SO4)2*12H2O}$) were in use since ancient Greece time.

a) The freezing point depression constant for water is $K_\mathrm{f} = 1.86\,^\circ\mathrm{C\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate the freezing point of the solution prepared by dissolving $9.48\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{KAl(SO4)2*12H2O}$ in $100.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water.

b) The most important ore of aluminium is bauxite, which consists from $\ce{Al2O3}$ and impurities. Bauxite can be purified by dissolving in concentrated $\ce{NaOH}$ solution. Write molecular equation that shows what is happening when $\ce{Al2O3}$ reacts with $\ce{NaOH}$ solution.

c) After removal of insoluble impurities, weak acid is added to the solution obtained in part b and $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ is precipitating. Solubility product $K_\mathrm{SP}$ for $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ is $1.3\cdot10^{-33}$ (at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Calculate mass of pure $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ that can be dissolved in $10.0\,\mathrm{L}$ of pure water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid or its salts) is among the most important and widely used reagents in titrimetry. Unfortunately, this reagent is not good for direct determination of aluminium ions, because EDTA reacts with aluminium ions too slowly. Problem can be solved by applying back titration method. In the beginning EDTA and aluminium compound solution are allowed to react in the hot solution for several minutes, and then excess EDTA can be fast and easily titrated with $\ce{Zn^{2+}(aq)}$. Analysis is performed in presence of buffer solution. Reactions taking place in this method can be represented as:

$$\ce{Al^{3+} + EDTA^{4-} -> Al*EDTA^-}$$

and

$$\ce{Zn^{2+} + EDTA^{4-} -> Zn*EDTA^{2-}}$$

d) $20.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of solution, that contains $\ce{Al^{3+}}$, was transferred into flask that contains $50.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $0.0500\,\mathrm{M}$ EDTA solution. Mixture was boiled for several minutes. For titration of the resulting mixture $23.25\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.0500\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ solution was necessary. Calculate molar concentration of $\ce{Al^{3+}}$ in the initial solution.

Trihalides of aluminium (like $\ce{AlCl3}$) are very strong Lewis acids and finds extensive use as catalysts. With some ligands L aluminium trichloride may form four-coordinated $\ce{AlCl3L}$ or even five-coordinated $\ce{AlCl3L2}$.

e) Assuming that L is a monodentate ligand, draw all possible geometrical isomers of $\ce{AlCl3L2}$.

f) In gas phase aluminium trichloride exists as $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ molecules with two bridging Cl atoms. Make a drawing that represents spatial structure of $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ molecule.

problems.title: Beware of light!
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Beware of light! (10 points)

Students found in a laboratory a bottle with little bit wet reagent $\mathbf{A}$, which had label „light sensitive”. Students have not paid attention to this label, and left the bottle on the bench over the summer break. As a result, the bottle was in direct sunlight for several hours a day. After the summer break students noticed that some changes happended to the content of the bottle. There were three compounds formed: $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is also used to increase solubility of $\mathbf{C}$ in aqueous solutions. In this process anion $\mathbf{E}$ is formed, which is also a part of compound $\mathbf{D}$. If concentrated solutions of $\mathbf{A}$ are mixed with concentrated solution $\mathbf{B}$ and then the obtained solution are allowed to react with some yellow-green gas $\mathbf{F}$, two new compounds are formed. Of this mixture, compound $\mathbf{G}$ in acidic media reacts with $\mathbf{A}$, which leads to $\mathbf{C}$ as one of the products. Oxygen content in compound $\mathbf{G}$ is 22.4% (by mass). If compound $\mathbf{G}$ reacts with the acid derived from $\mathbf{F}$, which consist of only two elements, the reaction leads to $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{F}$ and two other products.

1. Provide formulae for compounds $\mathbf{A}$ - $\mathbf{G}$ and reaction equations for all mentionned proceses.

2. Why $\mathbf{A}$ is light sensitive and nothing happens if it is stored in the dark? Mark correct answer(-s).

• a. light is form of activation energy provided
• b. light initiates electrolytic dissociation
• c. light initiates formation of radicals
• d. light is oxidizing agent
• e. light is reducing agent

3. Why the solubility of $\mathbf{C}$ in water increases if compound $\mathbf{A}$ is added?

4. Draw the Lewis structure of anion $\mathbf{E}$.

5. Calculate maximum pH, at which a reaction between $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ still proceeds at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, if $[\mathbf{G}] = 0.25\,\mathrm{M}$ and $[\mathbf{A}] = 0.10\,\mathrm{M}$. $E^\circ(\mathbf{A}) = 0.536\,\mathrm{V}$, $E^\circ(\mathbf{G}) = 1.195\,\mathrm{V}$.

Before summer holidays started students used compound $\mathbf{A}$ for investigation of reaction kinetics. It is known that compound $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with persulphate ions ($\ce{S2O8^{2-}}$) forming compound $\mathbf{C}$ and sulphate ions. Investigating kinetics at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ temperature they obtained data of initial reaction rate $v_0$ depending on reactant concentrations $C_0$. These data are shown in table 1.

Table 1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} C_0(\ce{S2O8^{2-}}),\ \mathrm{mmol/L} & C_0(\mathbf{A}),\ \mathrm{mmol/L} & v_0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{mol/(L\times s)} \\ \hline 0.10 & 10 & 1.1 \\ 0.20 & 10 & 2.2 \\ 0.20 & 5.0 & 1.1 \end{array}$$

6. Write balanced chemical equation for reaction of persulphate ions with compound $\mathbf{A}$ (net ionic equation is also acceptable).

7. Determine reaction partial orders, write kinetic expression and calculate reaction rate constant at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

8. They found in literature that activation energy for this reaction is $42\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Calculate temperature (in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$) needed to increase reaction rate 10 times if reactant concentrations remains the same.

9. Calculate what time (in hours) is necessary to decrease reactant concentrations 10 times if initial concentrations for both reactants are equal with $1.0\,\mathrm{mmol/L}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ temperature.

problems.title: Ordinary Physical Chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Ordinary Physical Chemistry (7 points)

Part I. Initial conditions of the reaction $\ce{H2 + N2 -> NH3}$ is $n_0(\ce{H2}) = n_0(\ce{N2})$, $n_0(\ce{NH3}) = 0$. At $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{p}$ of the reaction is $1{,}60\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{bar^{-2}}$.

a) Write the equation of the reaction.

b) Express analytically the mole fraction $x(\ce{NH3})$ and $K_\mathrm{p}$ in terms of a ratio $y$, which is a fraction of the amount of produced ammonia to twice the initial amount of reagents, $y = n_\infty(\ce{NH3})/2n_0$ or $n_\infty(\ce{NH3}) = 2yn_0$.

c) Calculate the pressure (bar), under which the partial pressure of $\ce{NH3}$ equals 11.11% of total pressure.

Part II. Mixture of gases containing $\ce{CO}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{CH3OH}$ is blown over a catalyst at $500\,\mathrm{K}$.

d) Would methanol form in the reaction $\ce{CO + H2 -> CH3OH}$ under the given conditions: $p_{\ce{CO}} = 9p_{\ce{H2}} = 99p_{\ce{CH3OH}}$, $p_{\ce{CH3OH}} = 0.099\,\mathrm{bar}$, and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ = 21.21\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

$$\Delta_\mathrm{r}G = \Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ + RT\ln Q$$

e) Calculate the value of $Q$ when $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G = 0$. Is it the minimal or maximal value above or below which the equilibrium is shifted towards methanol production?

problems.title: Smart robot
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Smart robot (13 points)

The hero of the movie “Star Wars” – a very intelligent robot R2-D2 received $20.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ of radioactive sample $\mathbf{P}$ known to contain only element $\mathbf{A}$. Robot divided this sample into two halfs of equal masses. With the help of gas diffusion method he quickly separated the first half into two parts. He obtained two equal volumes of gasses (under appropriate contitions) which weights were $4.92$ and $5.08\,\mathrm{mg}$; activities equaled $5.19\cdot10^{13}$ and $2.94\cdot10^{13}$ decays per second, correspondigly. These two were isotopes of element $\mathbf{A}$. R2-D2 chlorinated the second half of the sample yielding higher chloride $\mathbf{B}$ which after hydrolysis in water gave a solution of triprotic acid $\mathbf{C}$ and strong acid $\mathbf{D}$. This solution was titrated with $19.95\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.1234\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ solution.

a) Write the chemical symbols for element $\mathbf{A}$ and formulas for compounds $\mathbf{B}$–$\mathbf{D}$.

b) Write four equations for the reactions mentioned above.

c) Provide calculations to confirm the validity of your solution.

d) By what time all the sample will have almost completely decayed, i.e. total remaining activity would be less than 0.1% of the initial one.

R2-D2 found that after this time the remaining $10.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ of sample $\mathbf{P}$ consisted of two isotopes of element $\mathbf{E}$. Robot could not resist the delight of chlorinating them. As a result he obtained yellow substance $\mathbf{F}$. When hydrolysed in water substance $\mathbf{F}$ formed diprotic weak acid $\mathbf{G}$, diprotic oxoacid $\mathbf{H}$, and acid $\mathbf{D}$. This solution was titrated with $2.136\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.4321\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ solution.

e) Write the chemical symbols for element $\mathbf{E}$ and formulas for compounds $\mathbf{F}$–$\mathbf{H}$.

f) Write five equations for chemical reactions and two reactions of radioactive decay of isotopes of element $\mathbf{A}$.

g) Provide calculations to confirm the validity of your solution.

Hint: Assume that molar mass of an isotope is an integer number.

problems.title: The hunt for the flat carbon
problems.problem:
Problem 6. The hunt for the flat carbon (13 points)

Incorporating a “flat” carbon atom in $\mathrm{sp^3}$ hybridization in a molecule would be very exciting achievement from theoretical point of view. Such geometry is associated with enormous amount of strain and it is a huge challenge to incorporate such element in a “stable” molecule.

A special class of compounds – fenestranes, could as well be an answer to this scientific challenge, although it must be noted that the most desirable symmetrical $\ce{C9}$ fenestrane, which could planar symmetry, is not yet synthesized.

The problem outlined below shows the synthesis of $\ce{C13}$ symmetrical fenestrane, even though bond angles in this molecule are distorted to a large extent, the planar symmetry around carbon atom is not achieved.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2011-6-fig1.png

• Bulky base = 2 equivalents of sterically crowded base like LDA (lithium diisopropilamide)
• Theoretical amount of base needed to obtain $\mathbf{D}$ is one mole
• The base used in deprotonation of $\mathbf{C}$ does not react with terminal alkyne
• $\mathbf{D}$ is formed in the initial $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction and contains phosphorus, under acidic workup conditions this compound is not stable and it converts into $\mathbf{E}$
• $\mathbf{E}$ is $\ce{C8}$ bicyclic compound.

Further carbon skeleton construction required the Pauson-Khand reaction (PKR). In general PKR involves alkyne, alkene and carbon monoxide. In the presence of cobalt catalyst PKR leads to a formation of cyclopentenone ring. Note! In order to apply PKR in the present synthesis, carbonyl group in $\mathbf{E}$ was removed to give $\mathbf{F}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2011-6-fig2.png

• $\mathbf{G}$ already possesses the carbon skeleton found in $\mathbf{J}$.
• $\mathbf{J}$ is very symmetrical.

1. Give structure of compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{J}$

2. Suggest a mechanism for transformation $\mathbf{D} \rightarrow \mathbf{E}$

problems.title: Silver compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Silver compounds

Silver forms sparingly soluble salts with chloride, bromide, iodine, and cyanide. Their $K_\mathrm{sp}$ values are $1.77\cdot10^{-10}$, $5.2\cdot10^{-13}$, $8.3\cdot10^{-17}$, and $5.97\cdot10^{-17}$, respectively.

a) Determine the order of precipitation of the anions in an equimolar solution. Assume that precipitation is the only reaction and that cyanide ions do not hydrolyze.

b) To what extent (in percent) have bromide ions precipitated by the time chloride ions start to precipitate?

c) Cyanide ions correspond to a weak acid hydrogen cyanide ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 9.21$) and are, therefore, hydrolyzed to a different extent depending on the pH of the solution. If the pH of the solution is 7.0, what extent of the cyanide ions has been hydrolyzed?

d) Determine the order of precipitation of the chloride, bromide, iodine, and cyanide anions in the equimolar solution (pH = 7.0) while accounting for the hydrolyses of $\ce{CN-}$ ions.

e) Is it possible to selectively (left into the solution less than 0.1% of the starting concentration) precipitate iodine so that other ions do not coprecipitate at pH = 7?

In the solutions with high halogen content, ammonia ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b} = 4.75$) is often added to avoid precipitation. In the solution, two possible complexes are formed:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Ag+ + NH3 <=> Ag(NH3)+} & K_\mathrm{f}[\ce{Ag(NH3)+}] = 2.1\cdot10^{3} \\ \ce{Ag(NH3)+ + NH3 <=> Ag(NH3)2+} & K_\mathrm{f}[\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}] = 1.7\cdot10^{7} \end{array}$$

f) Determine how much silver is not bound to the complexes if the solution contains 0.10 M $\ce{Ag+}$, 0.50 M ammonia, and the pH of the solution is 7.0.

g) How much silver can be dissolved in 0.10 M chloride solution that also contains 0.50 M ammonia and the pH is 7.0?

problems.title: Fortamine
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Fortamine

Antibiotic Fortamine has an interesting structure – all of its cyclohexane carbon atoms are chiral. You must deduce the absolute configuration for all of them (besides the other questions). The stereochemical information must be shown unambiguously for all the compounds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-2-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-2-fig2.png

The starting material $\mathbf{A}$ was treated with $m$-chloroperoxybenzoic acid, followed by methylamine to produce compound $\mathbf{B}$. a) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{B1}$, $\mathbf{B2}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{C1}$.

The conversion of $\mathbf{D}$ to $\mathbf{E}$ is a modification of a classical reaction, where a carboxylic acid is used instead of an ester. However, both the ester and acid would yield the same product $\mathbf{E}$. The latter was treated with a non-nucleophilic base DBU to give an elimination product $\mathbf{F}$.

Unlike $m$-CPBA and other peroxyacids, $\ce{CF3CO3H}$ is able to coordinate not only with hydrogen-bond donors but also to protect alcohols. In this case, it leads to a stereoselective reaction. Treatment of $\mathbf{G}$ with PhSNa followed by elimination gives compound $\mathbf{H}$, which, after a few subsequent reactions, is transformed into enantiomerically pure Fortamine.

problems.title: Redox flow battery
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Redox flow battery

A redox flow battery consists of two electrolyte tanks and two (usually carbon) electrodes, which are separated by a proton exchange membrane. One of the tanks contains an oxidizer aqueous solution and the other reducing agent aqueous solution. If the oxidation-reduction reactions are reversible, the system can be used as a rechargeable battery. Some high energy density flow battery systems are promising candidates as an energy source for an electric car.

In the case of the vanadium redox battery (VRB), both electrolytes contain vanadium redox species, which exist in oxidation states V, IV, III, and II. The cathode electrolyte with 1 M vanadium cation concentration was prepared by dissolving vanadium(V) oxide in 4 M sulfuric acid, yielding a hydrated cation with a molecular mass of $155\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. The anode electrolyte was prepared by electrochemical reduction of the cathode electrolyte.

During VRB discharging, the cathode electrolyte changes from yellow to green and, finally, blue; the anode electrolyte turns from violet to green.

If ammonium vanadate(V) is reduced with zinc in a sulfuric acid solution, the following color changes can be seen: yellow → green → blue → green → violet.

a) Deduce the reactions taking place during ammonium vanadate(V) reduction with zinc.

b) Identify redox compounds and write i) anode, ii) cathode, and iii) overall reaction during discharging of VRB.

c) i) Write a formula for calculating the EMF of the VRB cell as a function of vanadium redox potentials and concentration of cations. ii) How much does the voltage of VRB change when pH is one unit lower?

d) The experimental voltage of VRB is 1.4 V. Calculate i) Gibbs energy and ii) equilibrium constant $K$.

e) Calculate and compare the energy density of VRB with lead-acid battery ($40\,\mathrm{Wh\,kg^{-1}}$). For simplification, the volume of the VRB can be taken equal to the volume of electrolyte solutions with a density of $1.3\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

problems.title: Kinetics of neuromuscular enzyme
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Kinetics of neuromuscular enzyme

Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme in the neuromuscular junction that catalyzes the degradation of acetylcholine – a neurotransmitter released by the parasympathetic nervous system. Inhibitors of this enzyme are used in medicine to treat glaucoma and postural tachycardia syndrome. In this problem, the kinetics of this enzyme is analyzed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-4-fig1.png

It is known that the first step of this enzymatic reaction is the reversible binding of the acetylcholine (substrate, S) to the acetylcholinesterase (enzyme, E), producing enzyme-substrate complex (ES). The second step is the reaction itself and the release of the products (P) and free enzyme (E), and it is known that this is the rate-determining step.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-4-fig2.png

It is also known that this reaction obeys the Michaelis–Menten kinetics: $v = \dfrac{v_\mathrm{max}[S]}{K_\mathrm{M} + [S]}$, where $v_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum rate of the reaction and $K_\mathrm{M}$ is Michaelis constant.

a) By assuming that the enzyme-substrate complex is in a steady state, derive the Michaelis–Menten equation.

Using the Michaelis–Menten equation, determine reaction rate order with respect to the substrate in two cases: i) substrate concentration in solution is huge; ii) substrate concentration is very small.

b) Sketch the graph showing reaction rate dependence on the enzyme concentration.

The reaction rate is temperature-dependent.

c) Sketch two graphs showing reaction rate as a function of temperature in classical reaction (case i) and in enzymatic reaction (case ii).

In the experiment, the rate of this enzymatic reaction was measured at various acetylcholine concentrations. The results are shown as a plot of the inverse of the rate against the inverse of substrate (acetylcholine) concentration. Two data points are marked in the graph.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-4-fig3.png

d) Which method is more suitable for investigating acetylcholine hydrolysis reaction:

• i) gasometry;
• ii) gravimetry;
• iii) conductometry;
• iv) titrimetry?

e) Linearize the Michaelis–Menten equation to obtain an equation consistent with the data presented in the Figure.

f) Calculate $v_\mathrm{max}$ and concentration of the substrate at which the reaction rate is half the maximum.

g) Calculate the rate constant $k_2$., if the total concentration of acetylcholinesterase in the experiment was $2.00\cdot10^{-5}$ M.

The activity of acetylcholinesterase was tested in the presence of 3 different inhibitors:

• Physostigmine – competitive inhibitor used in the treatment of glaucoma;
• Caffeine – non-competitive inhibitor, effects of coffee partly originate from this inhibition; Caffeine can bind with both free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex, rate of both reactions is the same;
• A2435 – uncompetitive inhibitor which binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex.

The effects of these three inhibitors are shown in a plot of the inverse of rate against the inverse of substrate concentration with inhibitors ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$) and without an inhibitor ($\mathbf{N}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2014-4-fig4.png

h) Which of the lines $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, or $\mathbf{C}$ correspond to each of the inhibitors mentioned above?

There is another way of linearizing the Michaelis–Menten equation to a different form. In this form, plotting $[S]/v$ against $\mathbf{X}$ gives a straight line.

i) Determine the variable $\mathbf{X}$.

problems.title: Chemistry of superacids
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Chemistry of superacids

According to the classical definition, a superacid is an acid with an acidity greater than that of 100% sulfuric acid. According to the modern definition, a superacid is a medium in which the chemical potential of the proton is higher than in pure sulfuric acid.

The simplest class of superacids is the Brønsted superacids. The first acid named accordingly was chlorine-containing $\mathbf{A}$ because of its ability to protonate aldehydes and ketones. Due to its explosive hazard, its use is partially limited. By adding anhydrous $\mathbf{A}$ to concentrated nitric acid, salt $\mathbf{B}$ can be obtained.

a) Draw the chemical formula for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and the Lewis structure formulas for ions in $\mathbf{B}$. Draw all resonance structures of the cation in $\mathbf{B}$.

A superacid $\mathbf{C}$ is considered to be the strongest among superacids known so far and is prepared in a simple reaction between a Lewis superacid $\mathbf{D}$ and Brønsted superacid $\mathbf{E}$, both being binary compounds containing a common chemical element. The ratio of the weight fraction of this element in $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ is 2.1668. It is known that $\mathbf{C}$ is ionic and consists of two ions, $\mathbf{C}^{+}$ and $\mathbf{C}^{-}$.

b) Draw the chemical formulas and Lewis structures of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$. What is the geometrical shape of $\mathbf{D}$? Write equations of the described reactions.

c) Draw the chemical formula of $\mathbf{C}$. Draw the Lewis structures of $\mathbf{C}^{+}$ and $\mathbf{C}^{-}$. What is the geometrical shape of these ions?

This extraordinarily strong acid is able to protonate nearly all organic compounds. It has been shown it removes $\ce{H2}$ from isobutane (2-methylpropane) and methane from 2,2-dimethylpropane. Note that in this way, cation $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ is obtained.

d) Write the equations of these chemical reactions by showing the carbon atom that will be protonated. What considerations will determine which carbon atom gets protonated?

Recently, a group of scientists from Freiburg, Germany, reported the superacidity of $\mathbf{F}$, which is prepared in a simple reaction between a Brønsted acid $\mathbf{G}$ and a Lewis acid $\mathbf{H}$, both containing a common chemical element. It is known that the weight fraction of element $\mathbf{X}$ (not present in $\mathbf{G}$) in $\mathbf{H}$ is 0.10117, and also that $\mathbf{F}$ is ionic and its anion can exist in two chemically distinct forms for which molecular weight ratio $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}} : \mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{A}}$ is 1.7695.

e) Draw the chemical formula of $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{A}}$, $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{H}$. Draw the Lewis structures and predict the geometry of $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{A}}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. Draw the geometry of $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}}$.

$\mathbf{F}$ can protonate benzene by producing an ionic compound $\mathbf{J}$ containing anion $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}}$.

f) Write the chemical structure of $\mathbf{J}$. How many signals will there be in the $^{1}$H, $^{13}$C and $\mathbf{X}$ NMR spectra of $\mathbf{J}$?

Interestingly, the reaction between the Lewis acid $\mathbf{H}$ and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane produced an ionic compound $\mathbf{K}$ with the same anion $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}}$ and a cation $\mathbf{K}^{+}$.

g) Write the chemical structure of $\mathbf{K}$. How many signals will there be in the $^{1}$H, $^{13}$C and $\mathbf{X}$ NMR spectra of $\mathbf{K}$?

It has been shown that thermodynamic characteristics of ionic compounds similar to $\mathbf{K}$ can be calculated by the use of empiric equations. As input data, experimentally determined compound properties or those obtained from quantum chemical calculations can be used. Equations for calculation of vaporization, solvation (enthalpy for the transition from ions in the gas phase to ions in the liquid state), and lattice enthalpies are given below:

$$\Delta H_\mathrm{vap} = aV_\mathrm{m}^{2/3} + bH_\mathrm{g} + c;\quad \Delta H_\mathrm{solv} = -\Delta H_\mathrm{vap} - \Delta H_\mathrm{diss};\quad \Delta H_\mathrm{latt} = d\Delta H_\mathrm{solv} + e$$

$$a = -224\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,nm^{-2}},\quad b = 0.0929,\quad c = 194\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\quad d = -0.685,\ \text{and}\ e = 172\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

h) Use the provided equations (consistent with the Born–Haber cycle) to calculate the lattice enthalpy of $\mathbf{K}$, if $V_\mathrm{m}$ of $\mathbf{K}$ is $0.4175\,\mathrm{nm^3}$ (determined by single-crystal X-Ray diffraction), $H_\mathrm{g} = 394.9\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and $\Delta H_\mathrm{diss} = 395.9\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (both found by quantum chemical calculations).

The reaction between 0.100 mol of $\mathbf{H}$ and 0.100 mol of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane was performed in a calorimeter filled with $2.00\cdot10^{2}$ g of ethanol (specific heat capacity of $2.44\,\mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$). By performing the reaction at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it was found that the temperature of ethanol increased by $5.94\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while by performing the same reaction at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the temperature of ethanol increased by $2.46\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (assume the calorimeter constant to be 0 and enthalpy being temperature independent). It was determined that the melting point of $\mathbf{K}$ is $2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

i) Calculate the reaction enthalpy at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the enthalpy of fusion of $\mathbf{K}$.

j) Use the Born–Haber cycle to calculate the enthalpy of fusion of $\mathbf{K}$ from the results in question h). Identify the main cause of errors for each of the approaches used to determine the enthalpy of fusion.

The experimental enthalpy of vaporization of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane ($+32\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and the sublimation enthalpy of $\mathbf{H}$ ($+85\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) are tabulated in handbooks of physical chemistry.

k) Use the Born-Haber cycle to calculate the reaction enthalpy for the reaction between $\mathbf{H}$ and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in the gas phase (where separated ions $\mathbf{F}^{-}_{\mathbf{B}}$ and $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ in the gaseous state are obtained).

problems.title: Determination of water content
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Determination of water content (10 points)

Very small water quantities can be measured with different methods: Karl Fischer titration, nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared spectroscopy, gas chromatography, UV-Vis spectroscopy.

In Karl Fischer titration a mixture of iodine, pyridine (Py), sulfur dioxide and methanol is used. In the presence of water following reactions take place:

$$\ce{SO2 + CH3OH + H2O + I2 -> 2HI + CH3OSO3H}$$

$$\ce{Py + HI -> PyH^+I^-}$$

$$\ce{Py + CH3OSO3H -> PyH^+CH3OSO3^-}$$

Usually, the limiting component of the reaction is iodine.

As Karl Fischer titrant is somewhat unstable, the practical titre (mass of analyte per volume of titrant) is often determined right before the analyses of a sample. An analyst weighted 260.3 mg of pure water and filled the 100 ml volumetric flask with acetonitrile that does not contain any water. 10.00 ml of the sample was taken for analyses and 6.20 ml of titrant was spent to reach the endpoint.

1.1 Calculate the titre (mg/ml) of the Karl Fischer titrant.

The same titrant was used to determine the water content of commercial acetonitrile. 20.00 ml of the commercial acetonitrile was titrated with 5.12 ml of titrant. Density of acetonitrile is 0.786 g/ml.

1.2 Determine the water content in commercial acetonitrile (% and ppm).

A coulometric Karl Fischer titration is used in a laboratory, where one of the reagents $\ce{I2}$ is generated electrochemically from $\ce{I-}$. It was of interest what the bias of the coulometric titration is. 4.113 g of acetonitrile (containing an unknown amount of water) was analyzed with coulonometric Karl Fischer method and 138.7 C was passed through coulometer (1 C = 1 A·s). 143.2 mg of water was weighted into 100 ml volumetric flask and filled with the same acetonitrile to mark. 2.714 g of the sample was taken for analyses and 145.3 C was used for complete titration of the sample.

1.3 Calculate the bias for this titration. Faraday constant $F = 96500\,\mathrm{C/mol}$.

The same procedure was repeated with 1.356 g of water weighted into 100 ml volumetric flaks. For titrating 1.194 g of this sample 306.7 C was used.

1.4 Calculate the bias for this titration.

1.5 Explain why can two titrations have a significantly different bias in this case.

Karl Fischer titration can also be used for water determination in solid samples if these can be dissolved in appropriate solvent. However, some building material such as cement, chalk, ceramic materials can not be analysed in this way due to occurring side reactions.

Therefore, infrared spectroscopy was used. Two chalk based reference materials containing 2.1 mg/kg and 17.2 mg/kg of $\ce{H2O}$ were measured with attenuated total reflectance (ATR) method. At peak maximum absorptions observed were 0.045 and 0.371 AU (absorption units).

2.1 What side reaction occurs for these materials and how does it influence the bias of Karl Fischer method.

2.2 With IR-ATR method also a chalk sample was analysed and absorbance of 0.276 AU was recorded at the peak maximum. Based on the Lambert–Beer law calculate the water content in the chalk sample. Lamber Beer law: $A = \varepsilon l c$, where $A$ is the absorption at wavelength $\lambda$, $\varepsilon$ is the molar attenuation coefficient at wavelength $\lambda$, $l$ is the optical path length and $c$ is the analyte concentration. Assume that optical path length is the same for all three measured materials.

problems.title: Harpoons and collisions
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Harpoons and collisions (12 points)

When modeling the path of a single atom A, it is useful to use it as a point of reference and “freeze” all the other species in their own places. Therefore, we only have to consider any other particles when they collide with the atom whose path we are modelling. If a centre of another species B is located in such a way that the atom A will hit it, it is said to be in the collision tube of the atom A.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2015-4-fig1.png

1. Given that a golf ball with a radius of 2.3 cm is touching a basketball with a radius of 12.5 cm, calculate the distance between their centres.

2. Hence, calculate the radius ($R$, in meters) and area ($\sigma$, in square meters) of the cross section of the collision tube created by a gaseous potassium atom moving through bromine gas. The radius of a potassium atom is 243 pm and the “radius” of a bromine molecule is 165 pm.

The collision tube as a model is used in the kinetic theory of gases. By applying this model, a useful equation for the rate constant of second order reactions can be obtained:

$$k_2 = \sigma \bar{c} N_A e^{-\frac{E_A}{RT}},$$

where $\bar{c}$ is the average effective velocity of the gas molecules. The pre-exponential term describes the number of collisions occurring, while the exponential term describes the proportion of successful collisions

3. Write down the more popular form of this equation and name the scientist who proposed it

4. A second order reaction has a rate constant of $1000\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, an effective cross sectional area of the collision tube of $1.0{*}10^{-18}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, and average effective velocity of gas molecules of $100\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in standard conditions. What is the activation energy of the reaction in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$?

5. Consider a reaction whose activation energy is 0 J. Mark each correct statement with a + sign and each incorrect statement with a - sign. (Note: each incorrect answer will incur negative marks, with the total for this question not less than 0)

• An appropriately selected catalyst would speed up this reaction
• Every reactant atom/molecule has sufficient energy for the reaction
• The reaction enthalpy change has to be zero or negative
• The reactants of such a reaction are likely to be charge free and only contain paired electrons

6. Referring back to the beginning of the problem, calculate the $k$ ($\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$) of the reaction between gaseous potassium and bromine at 800°C. Assume that the activation energy of the reaction is 0 J. $\bar{c} = \sqrt{\frac{8k_\mathrm{B}T}{\pi\mu}}$, where $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant ($1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{m^2\,kg\,s^{-2}\,K^{-1}}$) and $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the particles involved ($\mu = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$).

However, the measured $k$ of the reaction is larger than the calculated value at $1.0\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, which seemingly suggests that more species react than actually collide. This is because of the so-called harpoon mechanism – the potassium atom “shoots” an electron into the bromine molecule even before the collision takes place. This occurs due to the fact that the cross-sectional area ignores the effect of the geometry of collisions on the reaction, as it assumes that all collisions in most cases are equal.

7. Assess how the transfer of the electron impacts the size of the particles and thus the cross-sectional area of the collision tube! (Note: each incorrect answer will incur negative marks, with the total for this question not less than 0)

7.1. What is the effect of ionisation of the K atom on its size?

A. It increases, as loss of the charge of one electron weakens the attraction between nucleus and the electron cloud
B. It increases, as loss of the 4s orbital weakens the shielding experienced by other orbitals, thus diffusing them
C. It decreases, as the lost electron is the only one in 4th energy level
D. It decreases, as the volume of the orbital the electron occupies is lost

7.2. What is the effect of electron transfer to the bromine molecule on its size?

A. It increases, as the new electron occupies a bonding molecular orbital
B. It increases, as the new electron occupies a anti-bonding molecular orbital
C. It decreases, as the new electron occupies a bonding molecular orbital
D. It decreases, as the new electron occupies a non-bonding molecular orbital

7.3. What is the net effect of the electron transfer on the cross-sectional area of the collision tube?

A. It increases
B. It decreases
C. Insignificant effect
D. Not enough data to assess

The modified reactive cross section area $\sigma^*$ which should be used for reactions proceeding by a harpoon mechanism can be calculated from radius $R_h^*$ using equation:

$$\sigma^* = \pi(R_h^*)^2.$$

$R_\mathrm{h}$ describes the separation of centres of reacting species. There are three contributions to the energy of interaction between the colliding species: ionization energy of potassium (abbreviated as $I$), electron affinity of bromine gas ($E_\mathrm{EA}$) and Coulombic interaction (CI) energy between the ions when they have been formed given by equation:

$$\mathrm{CI} = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R_h}.$$

$R_h^*$ is a distance when all these three contributions to the energy are in balance and following equation is obeyed:

$$0 = I - E_\mathrm{EA} + \mathrm{CI}$$

Calculate the radius $R_h^*$ and reactive cross section area $\sigma^*$, if it is given that $I = 420\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$, $E_\mathrm{EA} = 250\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$, and vacuum permittivity constant $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2\cdot N^{-1}\cdot m^{-2}}$ and elementary charge $e = 1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

Usually to describe such a reactions a steric factor $P$ is introduced, which connects reactive cross section area $\sigma^*$ with collision cross section area $\sigma$ so that $\sigma^* = P\sigma$.
