Problem 2. Solubility

In the table below are ionic radii and standard reduction potentials ($\ce{Me^{n+}}$/Me) for a set of metals:

$$\begin{array}{r|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{Fe^{3+}} & \ce{Fe^{2+}} & \ce{Cu^{2+}} & \ce{Cu+} & \ce{Zn^{2+}} & \ce{Hg^{2+}} & \ce{Pb^{2+}} & \ce{Ag+} & \ce{Hg+} \\ \hline r_+\ [\text{Å}] & 0.55 & 0.61 & 0.73 & 0.77 & 0.74 & 1.14 & 1.19 & 1.15 & 1.19 \\ \hline E^\circ(\ce{Me^{n+}}/\mathrm{Me})\ [\mathrm{V}] & -0.04 & -0.45 & +0.34 & +0.52 & -0.76 & +0.85 & -0.13 & +0.80 & +0.80 \end{array}$$

Enthalpy change of the metal-iodide solvation ($\ce{MeI}_n\mathrm{(s)} \rightarrow \ce{Me^{n+}}\mathrm{(aq)} + n\ce{I-}\mathrm{(aq)}$) can be roughly estimated using Latimer and Kapustinskii equations:

$$\Delta H_\mathrm{solv} = A\cdot\frac{|z_+|^2}{r_+ + r_O} + n\Delta H_\mathrm{hyd}(I^-) - B\cdot\frac{v\cdot|z_+|\cdot|z_-|}{r_+ + r_-}$$

where $A = -610\ \mathrm{kJ}\ \text{Å}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $B = -1080\ \mathrm{kJ}\ \text{Å}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $r_0 = 0.50\ \text{Å}$, $v$ is the number of ions in the empirical formula, $z_+$ and $z_-$ are the charges on the cation and anion, respectively, in elementary charges, and $r_+$ and $r_-$ are the radii of the cation and anion, respectively, in Å, $\Delta H_\mathrm{hyd}(\ce{I-}) = -308\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The radius of the iodide is 2.06 Å.

The entropy change of the metal-iodide solvation can be estimated using Sackur-Tedore and Powell-Latimer equations:

$$\Delta S_\mathrm{solv} = C + n\Delta S_\mathrm{hyd}(I^-) - D\cdot\frac{|z_+|}{(r_+ + r_\mathrm{dip})^2} - E\cdot \ln M_+$$

where $C = 88\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $D = 644\ \mathrm{J}\ \text{Å}^2\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $r_\mathrm{dip} = 1.30\ \text{Å}$, $E = 12.5\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $M$ is the molar mass of the cation, $\Delta S_\mathrm{hyd}(\ce{I-}) = -58.1\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

a) Show with calculations that for $\ce{CuI}$ $\Delta G_\mathrm{solv} > 0$, while for $\ce{CuI2}$ $\Delta G_\mathrm{solv} < 0$.

b) Which of the following iodides are insoluble in water: $\ce{FeI2}$, $\ce{CuI}$, $\ce{ZnI2}$, $\ce{HgI2}$, $\ce{PbI2}$, $\ce{AgI}$, $\ce{HgI}$.

In aqueous solution, $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ reduce $\ce{I-}$ to $\ce{I2}$. $E^\circ(\ce{I2}/\ce{I-}) = 0.535\ \mathrm{V}$.

c) Calculate the standard reduction potential for $\ce{Fe^{3+}}/\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and show that the reduction of $\ce{I-}$ to $\ce{I2}$ by $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ is spontaneous under standard conditions.

d) Calculate the standard reduction potential for $\ce{Cu^{2+}}/\ce{Cu+}$ and show that the reduction of $\ce{I-}$ to $\ce{I2}$ by $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ is spontaneous. $K_\mathrm{sp}(\ce{CuI}) = 1.1\cdot10^{-12}$.

problems.title: Nickel knickknackery
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Nickel knickknackery

By exploring the deepest corners of his table drawers, a student Dominykas (respectfully called Cheminykas by his friends) found a bottle containing a green crystalline substance with a writing $\ce{NiCl2.6H2O}$. It might be due to the never-coming spring, mesmerized by the greenery of this substance, Cheminykas decided to carry out a few experiments with this material.

After dissolving it in water, he treated the solution with concentrated ammonia solution, the odor of which might wake even the heaviest sleeper from the deepest winter hibernation. A colorful metal-ammine complex is formed when the reaction takes place.

$$\ce{NiCl2.6H2O + 5NH3 -> [Ni(NH3)5(H2O)]Cl2 + 5H2O}$$

Several colorful crystals have formed, were filtered, dissolved in $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of water, poured into the spectrophotometric cuvette and placed into the spectrophotometer. After registering the UV-Vis spectrum, Cheminykas observed that the most intense absorbance occurred at 394 nm wavelength. Wanting to explore this material more thoroughly, he decided to carry out a photometric analysis.

Consequently, he dissolved 0.2017 g of obtained colorful crystals in $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ water and poured this solution into a photometric cuvette with a 5.00 cm optical path length. The device showed that the solution transmitted only 0.7% of light. Knowing that the device is not very accurate at this part of the scale, he transferred the solution from the cuvette into a volumetric flask, diluted it to $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, and again transferred $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of this solution to the same photometric cuvette. This time, the device showed that 13.5% of light was transmitted.

a) Calculate the molar absorption coefficient of this material.

The color wheel is a simplified but effective visual tool to predict the absorbance bands without having to use a spectrophotometer.

b) Determine the colors of substances $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2017-4-fig1.png

Three absorption bands in the UV-VIS spectrum are usually observed for the coordination compounds of octahedral geometry, given in the descending order of transition energy: ${}^3\mathrm{T}_{1g}(\mathrm{P}) \leftarrow {}^3\mathrm{A}_{2g}$, ${}^3\mathrm{T}_{1g}(\mathrm{F}) \leftarrow {}^3\mathrm{A}_{2g}$ and $\mathrm{T}_{2g} \leftarrow {}^3\mathrm{A}_{2g}$.

c) Calculate the difference between ${}^3\mathrm{T}_{1g}$ ($\mathbf{F}$) $\leftarrow {}^3\mathrm{A}_{2g}$ transition energies of $\ce{[Ni(en)3]^{2+}}$(en – ethylenediamine) (substance $\mathbf{A}$) and $\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]^{2+}}$ (substance $\mathbf{B}$), providing an answer in electronvolts (eV).

Later on, Cheminykas heated the $\ce{NiCl2.6H2O}$ salt to remove water and treated it with dry dimethylammonium chloride to synthesize another compound $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$ bis(dimethylammonium) tetrachloronickelate(II), the coordination number of which is 6.

Having completed the synthesis, he took some of the material for characterization but carelessly left the remaining material on the heating plate. When the temperature rose to $110\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the color of the substance changed from red (substance $\mathbf{D}$) to deep blue (substance $\mathbf{E}$). Cheminykas quickly noticed that and turned off the heating plate. He further noticed that while the substance was cooling down to room temperature, the color of it changed again from blue to yellow (substance $\mathbf{F}$). Even more so, in two weeks, it returned to its original red color while being stored at room temperature.

Genuinely interested in this phenomenon, Cheminykas carried out literature research and found out that materials that possess an ability to reversibly change their color according to their temperature are called thermochromic, and the phenomenon itself is called thermochromism. He raised a few hypotheses to explain the thermochromic behavior of $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2017-4-fig2.png

d) Which of the following statements best describes the color change of $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$ upon heating?

• A. With an increasing temperature, enough energy is passed to the material to surpass the activation energy of reforming crystal lattice and formation of a more thermodynamically stable $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$ stereoisomer.
• B. A decomposition reaction of organic ligands is taking place, followed by a change in the chemical composition of the coordination compound.
• C. Because of the increased temperature, hydrogen bonds are weakened, and an infinite two-dimensional structure is destroyed, accompanied by the shift from octahedral to tetrahedral coordination geometry.
• D. The temperature excites the electrons in $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ d-orbitals, enabling the electronic transitions within the semiconductor bandgap.

e) Draw all possible coordination stereoisomers of $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$. If there are any optically active stereoisomers (enantiomers) – mark them.

f) Schematically depict the absorbance spectra of thermochromic nickel coordination compound before heating (substance $\mathbf{D}$), at thermochromic shift temperature (substance $\mathbf{E}$) and after cooling back to room temperature (substance $\mathbf{F}$). Only one absorption band per material is required to draw.

g) Compared with the $\ce{((CH3)2-NH2)2[NiCl4]}$ at thermochromic shift temperature, after cooling to room temperature, the required energy for d-d electronic transitions is:

• A. Lower than at thermochromic shift temperature.
• B. Higher than at thermochromic shift temperature.
• C. Same as at thermochromic shift temperature.

Finally, Cheminykas decided to treat the thermochromic nickel complex with some bromine and ethylenediamine ($\ce{H2N-CH2-CH2-NH2}$, en) which is a common bidentate ligand in coordination chemistry. He obtained a compound $\ce{[NiBrCl(en)2]}$, the coordination number of which is 6.

h) Draw all possible coordination stereoisomers of $\ce{[NiBrCl(en)2]}$. If there are any optically active stereoisomers (enantiomers) – mark their pairs.

Problem 5. Cleaning oil pipes

As wells are drilled in deeper and deeper waters, the accumulation of paraffin, asphaltene and hydrates is increasing due to the extremely low temperatures on the ocean floor. Removing the wax from wells and pipelines will entail additional costs such as the use of deep-water divers and special equipment to cut and remove paraffin build-up from the pipelines.

One simpler solution is to melt paraffin. A reaction between ammonium chloride and sodium nitrite has been proposed to achieve this (reaction 1).

a) Calculate the standard enthalpy of the reaction if the enthalpies of formation are: $\Delta H_\mathrm{f}(\ce{NaNO2}) = -359.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta H_\mathrm{f}(\ce{NH4Cl}) = -314.43\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta H_\mathrm{f}(\ce{NaCl}) = -411.12\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta H_\mathrm{f}(\ce{H2O}) = -285.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

b) We know that the equilibrium constant of reaction 1 is $K \approx 10^{60}$. What can we say about reaction 1 based on this information and the previous calculations? Choose which of the following statements is the most correct.

• i) The reaction is endothermic and reversible.
• ii) The reaction is exothermic and irreversible.
• iii) The reaction is endothermic and irreversible.
• iv) The reaction is exothermic and reversible.

To use reaction 1 in the oil industry, it is necessary to know the reaction rate and mechanism. Research Group I thought that the reaction was of the second order and that the rate-limiting step was the reaction of nitrosyl ion ($\ce{NO+}$) with molecular ammonia. The temperature dependence of the reaction between ammonium chloride ($c_0 = 0.5\ \mathrm{M}$) and sodium nitrite ($c_0 = 0.5\ \mathrm{M}$) was investigated in the temperature range 4–50 °C at pH 4, 5 and 6. As expected, the reaction rate followed the Arrhenius equation.

problems.title: Nobel medals
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Nobel medals (8 points)

In 1930s the German-resident Jewish scientist James Franck and Hitler critic Max von Laue smuggled their Nobel medals over the Danish border for safekeeping in Niels Bohr’s lab. When Copenhagen fell to the Nazis in April 1940, the medals and their keeper were no longer secure, so a Hungarian scientist from the lab, George de Hevesy, took it upon himself to hide them. He decided against burying them in the garden, and instead used a chemical trick.

He dissolved the medals in aqua regia (3:1 mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids) forming a tetracoordinate gold-containing monovalent anion $\mathbf{A}$ and a gas $\mathbf{B}$, as well as a hydronium ion and water. The vessel containing this orange-coloured solution was labelled “aqua regia” and hidden in the lab among the other chemicals. Though Nazis thoroughly searched the lab, they found no evidence of medals, which were kept in their dissolved state for years. It is also known that $\mathbf{B}$ coexists with a colourless liquid $\mathbf{C}$, which starts to predominate upon cooling.

To recover the gold, excess aqua regia was boiled off and residue was obtained. It was then redissolved in hydrochloric acid to reduce the remaining nitric acid and the acid mixture was boiled off again. Each reduction step forms water and yellow mixture of two gasses: $\mathbf{D}$ and monoelemental $\mathbf{E}$. $\mathbf{D}$ undergoes further decomposition into $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$, which spontaneously oxidises to gas $\mathbf{B}$ in atmospheric oxygen. The cycle of adding more hydrochloric acid and evaporation is repeated until a strong acid $\mathbf{G}$ is formed as a yellow-orange crystalline solid, which liberates $\mathbf{A}$ upon dissolution in water. $\mathbf{G}$ was then reacted with a solution of sodium pyrosulphite $\ce{Na2S2O5}$ in water to precipitate gold as a brown powder, creating hydrochloric acid and $\mathbf{H}$ ($w_\mathrm{Na}<40\%$) as side products. The gold precipitate was remoulded into Nobel medals, which were presented back to their rightful owners in 1952.

2. Draw Lewis structures for compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ indicating the formal charges! Use VSEPR to determine their geometry at N centres and overall geometry if appropriate.

A compound’s spin-only magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons can be estimated with the formula $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.

b) Using the data from the Latimer diagram, prove by calculations that the most stable oxidation states of $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ in aqueous solution are I and III, respectively.

The standard reduction potential of $\ce{Me^{n+}}$ can be estimated as:

$$E^\circ = (\Delta H_\mathrm{atom} + \Delta H_\mathrm{ion} + \Delta H_\mathrm{hydr})/(nF) - 4.52\,\mathrm{V},$$

where $\Delta H_\mathrm{atom}$ is the atomization enthalpy change of Me, $\Delta H_\mathrm{ion}$ is the sum of ionization energies, and $\Delta H_\mathrm{hydr}$ is the hydration energy of $\ce{Me^{3+}}$ cation in water.

c) Tick the right assumption for the derivation of the given equation.

problems.title: Synthesis of Erythronolide B
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Synthesis of Erythronolide B (12 points)

Natural product synthesis is an important part of the organic chemistry. These products usually show high biological activities and thus are extremely interesting from the medicinal standpoint. However, syntheses of these molecules are not trivial, since they tend to have many stereocentres and wide diversity of functional groups (which is what makes then so selective as potential drugs). One of these compounds is Erythronolide B, a biochemical precursor of an antibiotic Erythromycin. Many famous organic chemists, like Woodward, Evans, Carreira, Hoffmann and Danishefsky have succeeded at synthesizing it. In this problem we will discuss the Elias Corey synthesis of Erythronolide B. The full synthesis is not shown here, but the first part was synthesizing - what Corey called – $\mathbf{The\ Fragment\ 11}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2018-6-fig1.png

In this synthesis the compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are all non-aromatic meso-compounds. The compound $\mathbf{D}$, although initially obtained as racemic mixture, is purified to a single enantiomer. The conversion $\mathbf{F} \to \mathbf{G}$ proceeds with inversion of the stereochemistry at the reaction center, but conversion $\mathbf{G} \to \mathbf{H}$ proceeds with retention of the stereochemistry at the reaction center.

1.) Show the structures of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{M}$. For all the compounds $\mathbf{D}$ – $\mathbf{M}$, show the stereochemistry (R and S assignment is not necessary). [$\mathbf{G}$ is asked with stereochemistry.]

2.) Propose a mechanism for the conversion $\mathbf{M} \to$ $\mathbf{Fragment\ 11}$. You can do a schematic mechanism, as long as you show all the necessary features that describe the selectivity.

problems.title: Some chemistry of element X
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Some chemistry of element X (9 points)

Element $\mathbf{X}$ is very important to industry, where it is primarily used to manufacture semiconductor electronic devices and as an additive to lead alloys. Not long ago, different compounds of $\mathbf{X}$ were also used as pesticides and even as green pigments in paint, but these practices had to be abandoned due to the toxicity of $\mathbf{X}$. Various minerals of this element are present in the Earth’s crust and the majority of them are found in China. One such mineral is tennantite, which consists of three elements - Cu, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. Elements $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ can be found in groups 15 and 16 of the periodic table, respectively.

1) Identify the elements $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and determine the chemical formula of tennantite. Crystallographic data for the tennatite unit cell: lattice parameter $a = 10.186\,\text{Å}$, number of formula units per unit cell $Z = 2$, density $\rho = 4.6479\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Assume that the unit cell is cubic. Elemental composition by mass: $w_\mathrm{Cu} = 51.56\,\%$, $w_\mathbf{X} = 20.26\,\%$, $w_\mathbf{Y} = 28.18\,\%$. (6 points)

Let us consider the production of $\mathbf{X}$-containing compounds starting from this mineral.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-1-fig1.png

Thermal decomposition of tennantite leads to another mineral $\mathbf{A}$ with a highly symmetric structure, which consists of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ only. During the reaction, $\mathrm{Cu_2}\mathbf{Y}$ and vapours of $\mathbf{Y}$ are formed as by-products. Further oxidation of $\mathbf{A}$ leads to oxide $\mathbf{B}$ ($w_\mathbf{X} = 75.7\,\%$), which is a starting material for synthesis of almost all $\mathbf{X}$-containing compounds. Compound $\mathbf{C}$ reacts with $\ce{SbF5}$ in a 1:1 ratio to give salt $\mathbf{D}$ with an $\mathbf{X}$-containing cation and Sb-containing anion. $\mathbf{J}$, the anti-addition product of $\mathbf{F}$ to acetylene, is an organo-$\mathbf{X}$ compound known as Lewisite that has been manufactured for use in chemical weapons. In the reaction $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{G}$, sodium borohydride acts as a hydride donor. $\mathbf{K}$ is a semiconductor. $\mathbf{H}$ ($w_\mathrm{C} = 21.26\,\%$, $w_\mathrm{H} = 5.35\,\%$, $w_\mathbf{X} = 66.31\,\%$, $w_\mathrm{O} = 7.08\,\%$) is otherwise known as cacodyl oxide to obtain which potassium acetate has to react with $\mathbf{B}$. During the course of the reaction, evolution of a gas is observed and a potassium salt is formed as a by-product. 2 equivalents of the cacodylic acid $\mathbf{I}$ are obtained by oxidising 1 equivalent of $\mathbf{H}$.

2) a) Identify the formulas of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ (9 points)

b) draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{J}$. (6 points)

3) Write down balanced equations for all aforementioned reactions. (11 points)

• Tennantite $\rightarrow \mathbf{A}$
• $\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$
• $\mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{C}$
• $\mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{D}$
• $\mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{E}$
• $\mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{F}$
• $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{G}$
• $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{J}$
• $\mathbf{G} \rightarrow \mathbf{K}$
• $\mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{H}$
• $\mathbf{H} \rightarrow \mathbf{I}$

Similarly to heavy metal poisoning, patients having been in contact with $\mathbf{J}$ can be given chelation therapy. A famous example of a covalent drug used specifically in the case of Lewisite poisoning is 2,3-dimercaptopropan-1-ol, also known as British anti-Lewisite ($\mathbf{BAL}$).

4) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{BAL}$ and the product formed in its reaction with $\mathbf{J}$. Molar mass of the product is $M = 258.62\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. (3 points)

5) Using VSEPR theory, determine the geometries of the cation and anion of $\mathbf{D}$. (2 points)

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is useful beyond organic chemistry and can also be used in the study of inorganic species, although this can sometimes be more complicated due to line-broadening effects of quadrupolar nuclei (i.e nuclei with a spin quantum number $I$ greater than ½). Just like for protons ($I = ½$) in $^1$H NMR spectra of organic molecules, the number of lines in a multiplet can be predicted for any other NMR-active nucleus using the equation: $2nI + 1$, where $n$ is the number of coupling nuclei. The natural abundances of $^{19}$F ($I = 1/2$) and $\mathbf{X}$ ($I = 3/2$) are 100%. Two NMR-active nuclei of antimony exist: $^{121}$Sb ($I = 5/2$) and $^{123}$Sb ($I = 7/2$). The natural abundances of $^{121}$Sb and $^{123}$Sb are 57.25% and 42.75%, respectively. In the following questions, assume that any anisotropies resulting from cation-anion interactions average out over the experiment time course and only through-bond couplings are observed.

6) For solution-state NMR spectra of $\mathbf{D}$, predict the number of resonances and their theoretical splitting patterns in the a) $^{121}$Sb NMR spectrum, b) $\mathbf{X}$ NMR spectrum and c) $^{19}$F NMR spectrum. In your assignments, include the ratios of peak intensities for any multiplets as predicted by Pascal’s triangle. NB! There is no need to include integrals or any approximate chemical shifts. (8 points)

problems.title: Thermodynamics of electrochemical CO2 capture
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Thermodynamics of electrochemical $\ce{CO2}$ capture (10 points)

The electrochemical $\ce{CO2}$ capture is a promising technique for direct air capture, allowing to capture $\ce{CO2}$ from the atmosphere and then release it in pure concentrated form for further application. In this task, we will look at the electrochemical (Part I) and thermodynamical (Part II) basis for the capture process. Even though the text from Part I is relevant to Part II, Part II can be attempted without any results from Part I.

Part I - EMCS in the solution

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-2-fig1.png

One of the simplest systems is the electrochemically mediated complexation separation (EMCS), where the redox-active adsorbent is activated for the $\ce{CO2}$ capture at the cathode, while at the anode it is deactivated and releases $\ce{CO2}$. A more specific case is the EMCS in the solution, where the adsorbate is dissolved directly in the solution.

In the capture process, the first step is an electrochemical reaction

$$\mathrm{A(aq)} + m\,\mathrm{e^-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}^{m-}\mathrm{(aq)}$$

1. Using the Nernst equation write an expression for the reduction half-cell potential $E$.

Further the reduced $\mathrm{A}^{m-}$ is capturing $\ce{CO2}$

$$\mathrm{A}^{m-}\mathrm{(aq)} + m\,\mathrm{CO_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A(CO_2)}_m^{\,m-}\mathrm{(aq)}$$

2. Write an expression for the equilibrium constant $K$ for the given reaction, assuming the reference pressure $P_0$ to be 1.

For convenience we can define total adsorbent concentration - $A_0$:

$$A_0 = [\mathrm{A}] + [\mathrm{A}^{m-}] + [\mathrm{A(CO_2)}_m^{\,m-}]$$

And activated fraction $x_\mathrm{A'}$:

$$x_\mathrm{A'} = \left([\mathrm{A}^{m-}] + [\mathrm{A(CO_2)}_m^{\,m-}]\right)/A_0$$

We are now equipped to separate expression for half-cell potential $E$ into terms related to activated fraction and $\ce{CO2}$ pressure:

$$E = E^0 + RT/mF \cdot f_1(x_\mathrm{A'}) + RT/mF \cdot f_2(KP_\mathrm{CO_2}^{\,m})$$

3. Find expressions for $f_1(x_\mathrm{A'})$ and $f_2(KP_\mathrm{CO_2}^{\,m})$.

Now if we define $E_0$ to be potential when no $\ce{CO2}$ is present ($P_\mathrm{CO_2} = 0$), we can consider deviation potential $E^\mathrm{dev}$ observed at different $P_\mathrm{CO_2}$:

$$E^\mathrm{dev} = E(P_\mathrm{CO_2}) - E_0$$

4. Write an expression for $E^\mathrm{dev}$ in this case. (In case you could not do the previous question, provide the answer using $f_1(x_\mathrm{A'})$ and $f_2(KP_\mathrm{CO_2}^{\,m})$)

Part II - Thermodynamical analysis

To calculate the work needed to perform the capture-release cycle we have to consider a diagram analogous to that of the $p$-$V$ diagram known from classical thermodynamics. However, in this case, we consider a diagram $E^\mathrm{dev}$ vs. $\alpha$ (state of charge, which describes the relative amount of reduced species). To construct this diagram, we must first understand the relation between total $\ce{CO2}$ content ($x_\mathrm{CO_2}$, normalised with respect to A initial concentration) and partial pressure of $\ce{CO2}$ ($P_\mathrm{CO_2}$), which is given by the relation:

$$x_\mathrm{CO_2} = \alpha\cdot KP_\mathrm{CO_2}/(1 + KP_\mathrm{CO_2}) + k'_\mathrm{h,\,CO_2}P_\mathrm{CO_2}$$

The first term in the sum describes $\ce{CO2}$ which is bound to the reduced form of A, where $\alpha$ is the state of charge, which in the ECMS case coincides with the activated fraction $x_\mathrm{A'}$ defined before. The second term, however, describes the part of $\ce{CO2}$ that is dissolved in the solution, where $k'_\mathrm{h,\,CO_2}$ is normalised Henry constant.

In a specific example, let’s assume that $K = 500$, $P_\mathrm{CO_2} = 1\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $k'_\mathrm{h,\,CO_2} = 0.05\,\mathrm{bar^{-1}}$.

5. Calculate the total $\ce{CO2}$ content $x_\mathrm{CO_2}$ for cases $\alpha = 0.25$ and $\alpha = 0.75$.

During the $\ce{CO2}$ adsorption and desorption cycle, there are three types of thermodynamic pathways possible:

• Constant state of charge - $\ce{CO2}$ is adsorbed or released from A with no electrochemical reaction happening.
• Constant total $\ce{CO2}$ concentration - During the reduction/oxidation process the $\ce{CO2}$ in the solution adsorbs to the reduced species/adsorbed $\ce{CO2}$ is released into the solution, while the total $\ce{CO2}$ concentration remains constant.
• Constant $\ce{CO2}$ partial pressure - the external pressure is kept constant, therefore while the capture/release happens the total $\ce{CO2}$ concentration and state of charge change, while the partial pressure is constant.

The following plot shows the diagram of $E^\mathrm{dev}$ vs. $\alpha$. Solid lines indicate constant total $\ce{CO2}$ concentration ($x_\mathrm{CO_2}$ is constant), and dashed lines indicate constant $\ce{CO2}$ partial pressure ($P_\mathrm{CO_2}$ is constant). The labelled points A-F show special points during the capture-release cycle, which will be described later. Note, that you have already calculated the $x_\mathrm{CO_2}$ for points A and E in question 5 (or, if you haven’t, the precise values are not of particular interest).

6. Calculate the partial pressure $P_\mathrm{CO_2}$ at point C. (In case you could not calculate $x_\mathrm{CO_2}$ in the previous question, use a value $x_\mathrm{CO_2} = 0.35$)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-2-fig2.png

The release-capture system can be considered in two extremes. In both cases, the initial state of charge is 0.25, during adsorption, the partial pressure of the feed stream is 0.15 bar, and adsorption continues until the state of charge is 0.75. At the release stage, the $\ce{CO2}$ is released in a pure stream with a partial pressure of 1 bar.

Four-stage system:

• 1. As the absorbent is activated, i.e., the state of charge increases, while the total $\ce{CO2}$ concentration remains constant.
• 2. The activated absorbent is contacted with the feed gas until the partial pressure of the feed gas is reached.
• 3. The absorbent is deactivated as the state of charge decreases. In the end, the free $\ce{CO2}$ in the solution is at a partial pressure of 10 bar.
• 4. $\ce{CO2}$ is removed by desorption as a gas in the flash tank at a pressure of 1 bar

Two-stage system:

• 1. The adsorbent is activated and $\ce{CO2}$ is captured at the same time.
• 2. The adsorbent is deactivated and $\ce{CO2}$ is released at the same time.

7. Assign all the described steps with points shown in the $E^\mathrm{dev}$ vs. $\alpha$ diagram. (In the form: 1. X to Y)

The work required to perform the capture-release cycle is described as the area enclosed by the cycle in the $E^\mathrm{dev}$ vs. $\alpha$ diagram.

8. Tick the correct answer, consistent with your answer to the previous part.

• Four-stage system requires less work.
• Two-stage system requires less work.

problems.title: Solution ≠ liquid
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Solution ≠ liquid (12 points)

We are used to use term “solution” in the context of liquid materials. But solid solutions also exist. In solid solutions different atoms or ions form compounds with different stoichiometric composition, but the crystal lattice remains the same.

Ferrochrome has empirical formula $\mathrm{Fe}_x\mathrm{Cr}_{1-x}$ ($x$ – non-integer value). Both iron and chromium form body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal lattice, therefore their solid solution has the same lattice if a certain amount of iron atoms are substituted by chromium atoms in nodes of crystal lattice.

One ferrochrome cubic cell and five planar projections, perpendicular to z axis, are shown in Fig. 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1 Cubic cell of ferrochrome and its five planar projections along z axis.

1. Assuming that the cubic cell given in Fig. 1 corresponds to the composition of whole material, calculate the $x$ value in empirical formula $\mathrm{Fe}_x\mathrm{Cr}_{1-x}$.

2. The lattice parameter of the cell given in Fig. 1 is 576 picometers. Calculate the density of ferrochrome. Express the answer in $\mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$ dimensions.

3. The experimental ferrochrome density value differs by 5 % compared with the result you’ve calculated in question 2. Which of the following statements can explain such a difference? Circle correct answer letter(s)

a) Additional Fe or Cr atoms can be intercalated in octahedral or tetrahedral voids of the lattice

b) Formation of vacancies in nodes of crystal lattice

c) Because of random distribution of Fe and Cr atoms in the lattice one cubic cell does not ideally correspond to the actual composition of material

d) Chemical interactions between Fe and Cr cause the significant change of metallic radii of Fe and Cr atoms

e) In solid solutions lattice parameter values fluctuates significantly

Ionic solid solutions can be obtained by combining two or more ionic compounds. Substituting cations or anions of different charges in the lattice gives rise to peculiar physical properties of such material.

Forsterite is a mineral which has empirical formula $\ce{Mg2SiO4}$. Silicon is covalently bound to oxygen atoms and magnesium ions occupy octahedral holes in orthorhombic lattice. Reaction between forsterite and lanthanum (III) oxide yields $\mathrm{La}_x\mathrm{Mg}_y\mathrm{SiO_4}$ solid solution and one more byproduct, which contains no lanthanum.

4. Write chemical formula of byproduct.

5. Express index $y$ as a function of $x$.

6. When $\ce{La^{3+}}$ ions substitute $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ions, a certain concentration of vacancies are formed. Vacancies influence electrical conductivity of ionic solid solution. Which electric charge transfer mechanism occurs in $\mathrm{La}_x\mathrm{Mg}_y\mathrm{SiO_4}$ solid solution? Circle one correct answer letter.

a) $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ node

b) $\ce{La^{3+}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{La^{3+}}$ node

c) $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ node

d) $\ce{O^{2-}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{O^{2-}}$ node

e) $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ or $\ce{La^{3+}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ or $\ce{La^{3+}}$ node

f) $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, $\ce{La^{3+}}$ or $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, $\ce{La^{3+}}$ or $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ node

g) $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, $\ce{La^{3+}}$, $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ or $\ce{O^{2-}}$ migrates to the vacancy, a new vacancy is formed in $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, $\ce{La^{3+}}$, $\ce{Si^{4+}}$ or $\ce{O^{2-}}$ node

h) Free electrons migrate from vacancy to vacancy

7. By performing electrical conductivity measurements it was calculated that concentration of vacancies in lanthanum-doped forsterite is $6.2\cdot10^{17}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. Density of the material is $3.223\,\mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$. One unit cell contains one silicon and four oxygen atoms. Calculate index $x$ in formula $\mathrm{La}_x\mathrm{Mg}_y\mathrm{SiO_4}$ by assuming that all vacancies are formed because of $\ce{La^{3+}}$–$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ exchange.

Cations can intercalate in ionic compounds via different mechanisms. For example, ferrous oxide $\ce{FeO}$ can react with lithium oxide $\ce{Li2O}$ to yield a solid solution $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{O}$. During the reaction, a fraction of iron atoms oxidize to +3 oxidation state. One of the simplest methods to analyze the composition of such solid solution is electrochemical $\ce{Fe^{3+}}/\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ratio determination. We denote the ratio $r = \frac{n(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}})}{n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}})}$, where $n(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}})$ ir $n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}})$ are molar amounts of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ respectively. Reciprocal values of empirical formula index $x$ and ratio $r$ are related linearly ($a$ and $b$ – integer numbers):

$$\frac{1}{x} = a\cdot\frac{1}{r} + b$$

8. Calculate values $a$ and $b$.

When $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{O}$ is dissolved in non-oxidizing acid, an excess of sodium cyanide is added to bind all iron atoms to $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}}$ and $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{3-}}$ complex ions. Two electrodes are immersed in this solution: a working Pt electrode and reference $\mathrm{AgCl|Ag,\,Cl^-}$ electrode, filled with saturated KCl solution. 0.092 V potential difference is measured at the starting moment of experiment, then an increase of $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}}$ concentration was observed. Redox potentials at 298 K and 1 bar are:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{AgCl(s) + e^- -> Ag(s) + Cl^-(aq)} & E = E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag,\,Cl^-}) - \dfrac{RT}{F}\ln[\mathrm{Cl^-}]_\mathrm{saturated} = +0.197\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{3-}(aq) + e^- -> [Fe(CN)6]^{4-}(aq)} & E^\circ = +0.370\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

9. Calculate the ratio $r$ and index $x$ from electrochemical measurement data.

Organic solid solutions are attractive because of their optical properties. For instance, p-bromobenzaldehyde derivatives weakly phosphoresce (emit light) in crystalline state. But if p-bromobenzaldehyde derivative ($\mathbf{A}$) is co-crystallized with 1,4-dibromobenzene ($\mathbf{B}$), a solid phosphorescent solution forms. $\mathbf{B}$ molecules interrupt interactions between $\mathbf{A}$ molecules and does not allow for vibrational relaxation of excited $\mathbf{A}$ molecules. This solid solution has primitive orthorhombic structure, where nodes can be occupied by either $\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{B}$ (Fig. 2 (a)).

A simple kinetic model can be used to estimate phosphorescence intensity $I$ of the material:

$$I = \frac{CN\cdot k_{ph}}{k_{ph}\cdot r_0^2 + k_{vib}\cdot\sum_i\left(CN_i^2\cdot r_i^2\right)}$$

$CN$ – coordination number, defining average count of $\mathbf{A}$ molecules around selected $\mathbf{A}$ molecule. $k_{ph}$ and $k_{vib}$ are phosphorescence and vibrational relaxation rate constants, $r_0$ is a constant and $CN_i$ are average counts of $\mathbf{A}$ molecules, that are at a specific $r_i$ distance from selected $\mathbf{A}$ molecule. $r_0$ and $r_i$ must be expressed in angstrems (Å) and $CN$, $CN_i$ and $r_i$ values should be considered only for the first coordination shell (nearest atoms, Fig. 2 (b)).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2 (a) Primitive orthorhombic cell with parameters $a$, $b$, $c$ and nodal positions marked as red balls; (b) if yellow molecule is the selected one, blue molecules are in the first coordination shell.

10. Show that for orthorhombic lattice with different unit cell lengths $a$, $b$, $c$ phosphorescence intensity can be calculated using formula below.

$$I = \frac{9\cdot CN\cdot k_{ph}}{9\cdot k_{ph}\cdot r_0^2 + k_{vib}\cdot CN^2\cdot(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)}$$

11. Solid solution $\mathbf{X}$ is prepared by co-crystallising $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in ratio $n(A):n(B) = 1:1$. Solid solution $\mathbf{Y}$ is prepared by co-crystallising $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in ratio $n(A):n(B) = 2:1$. $\mathbf{X}$ phosphoresce 1.25 times more intensely than $\mathbf{Y}$. Calculate the length of the diagonal of orthorhombic unit cell, if $\frac{k_{ph}}{k_{vib}} \approx 10^{-4}$ and $r_0 \approx 710\,\text{Å}$.

problems.title: Total synthesis of (–)-Colombiasin A
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Total synthesis of (–)-Colombiasin A (10 points)

(–)-Colombiasin A is a marine natural product first isolated from a species of coral found off the coast of San Andres island, Colombia. Following the initial reported total synthesis and structural assignment by K. C. Nicolaou and co-workers in 2001, Colombiasin A and structurally closely related compounds have been prepared via numerous different synthetic approaches. Construction of the carbon skeleton poses in this case some rather unique challenges to the synthetic chemist. Most notably, the two adjacent quaternary carbons central to Colombiasin A’s carbacycles have been recognised as some of the most challenging aspects of building this natural product.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-5-fig1.png

In this task, you will follow the approach of D. C. Harrowven and co-workers, which starts off simple, yet concludes in a spectacular fashion. The synthesis begins from enantiomerically pure dihydrocarvone. In the first half of the sequence, a number of simple transformations eventually lead to an $E$/$Z$ mixture of conjugated diene $\mathbf{E}$. The stereochemical configurations of compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ have been provided in the scheme below. In reaction $\mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{D}$, a partial reduction occurs over steps 2i)–ii). It is also known that both $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ contain a secondary hydroxyl group.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-5-fig2.png

1) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$, taking stereochemistry into account. (9 points)

2) From the list below, tick the most suitable solvent for the reaction $\mathbf{C}$ + NaCN. (2 points)

• $n$-hexane
• toluene
• $\ce{NH3(l)}$
• 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE)
• dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO)
• kefir
• 1:1 $\ce{MeOH}/\ce{H2O}$ with 5% v/v $\ce{H2SO4}$

3) Sketch the reaction mechanism for transformation $\mathbf{D} \rightarrow \mathbf{E}$ and clearly indicate the three by-products formed in progress. You may abbreviate parts of molecule(s) irrelevant to this transformation. Hint: the reaction proceeds via an anionic spirocyclic intermediate. Spiro compounds are molecules, which contain at least two ring systems with only a single common atom. (8 points)

4) Explain briefly, with reference to relevant $^3J_\mathrm{H\text{-}H}$ coupling constants, how the $E$/$Z$ isomeric ratio of compound $\mathbf{E}$ could be estimated by $^1$H NMR spectroscopy. (3 points)

In the next part of the synthesis, the $E$/$Z$ mixture of compound $\mathbf{E}$ is first oxidised into $\mathbf{F}$ and subsequently, with the aid of catalytic $\ce{I2}$, converted into stereochemically pure $\mathbf{G}$. Compound $\mathbf{G}$ is then subjected to an interesting sequence of reactions. First, an alkenyllithium species is formed in situ from $\mathbf{G}$ via a Shapiro reaction, which then undergoes a nucleophilic addition to compound $\mathbf{X}$. Following aqueous work-up, the α-hydroxy ketone $\mathbf{H}$ is obtained. Hint: the first step in the Shapiro reaction is formation of a hydrazone via condensation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-5-fig3.png

Information about compound $\mathbf{X}$:

• Elemental composition: C - 64.27 %; H - 7.19 %; O - 28.54 %.
• $^1$H NMR (300 MHz, $\ce{CDCl3}$): δ 2.19 (s, 1H), 1.62 (s, 3H) ppm. NB! The listed integrals are relative not absolute.
• $^{13}$C NMR (75 MHz, $\ce{CDCl3}$): δ 199.9, 195.9, 192.8, 182.7, 87.5, 28.7, 9.3 ppm.
• Selected IR spectroscopic data: $\nu_\mathrm{max}$ ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) - 1799, 1748, 1584, 1395.

5) Identify the four low molecular weight by-products formed in step $\mathbf{E} \rightarrow \mathbf{F}$. (2 points)

6) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$, compound $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{H}$, taking stereochemistry into account where applicable. (8 points)

The total synthesis of (−)-Colombiasin A from dihydrocarvone culminates in an impressive cascade, which proceeds from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{K}$ via intermediates $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$. In the very last steps, a [4+2] cycloaddition furnishes the (−)-Colombiasin A core and deprotection using $\ce{BF3}$ etherate reveals the target molecule.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2022-5-fig4.png

problems.title: Determination of protein content by Kjeldahl method
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Determination of protein content by Kjeldahl method (44 points, 10% of total)

The Kjeldahl method was developed in 1883 by the Danish chemist Johan Kjeldahl. It was designed to determine the nitrogen content in organic compounds. Although 140 years have passed, this method is still used to determine protein content in food. The method consists of three stages: digestion, distillation, titration, and calculations.

I. Digestion stage

At the digestion stage, nitrogen in a sample is converted into ammonium ions. Digestion is achieved by adding excess concentrated sulfuric acid to the sample and boiling the mixture for a few hours.

1.1 (4 pt) Write the balanced equation for the reaction between heated concentrated sulfuric acid and: a) C, b) S.

1.2 (2 pt) Will boiling concentrated sulfuric acid convert nitrate ions into ammonium ions? Circle the correct answer: Yes / No.

Concentrated sulfuric acid is a 98% $\ce{H2SO4}$ solution. Interestingly, pure, anhydrous sulfuric acid contains not only $\ce{H2SO4}$ molecules. As the equilibrium is reached, $\ce{HSO4-}$; $\ce{HS2O7-}$; $\ce{H2S2O7}$; $\ce{H3O+}$; $\ce{H3SO4+}$ are also found.

1.3 (4 pt) Fill in the table by entering formulas.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Compound} & \text{Quantity (mmol) in 1 kg pure } \ce{H2SO4} \\ \hline \underline{\qquad\qquad} & 14.9 \\ \underline{\qquad\qquad} & 11.3 \\ \ce{H3O+} & 8.0 \\ \ce{HS2O7-} & 4.4 \\ \underline{\qquad\qquad} & 3.6 \end{array}$$

1.4 (2 pt) Tick the correct answer.

• The addition of NaCl and/or $\ce{Na2SO4}$ will increase the boiling point of $\ce{H2SO4}$. There is little to no difference if NaCl or $\ce{Na2SO4}$ is used.
• The addition of NaCl will increase the boiling point of $\ce{H2SO4}$. For faster digestion it is significantly better to add NaCl than $\ce{Na2SO4}$.
• The addition of $\ce{Na2SO4}$ will increase the boiling point of $\ce{H2SO4}$. For faster digestion it is significantly better to add $\ce{Na2SO4}$ than NaCl.
• The addition of NaCl and/or $\ce{Na2SO4}$ will reduce the boiling point of $\ce{H2SO4}$.
• The addition of NaCl and/or $\ce{Na2SO4}$ will reduce the boiling point of $\ce{H2SO4}$, however, salt will act as a catalyst.

II. Distillation stage

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2023-1-fig1.png

At the distillation stage, the solution from the digestion stage with formed $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$, is exposed to an excess of NaOH solution. Ammonium ions react with hydroxide ions:

$$\ce{NH4+ + OH- <=> NH3 + H2O} \qquad (1)$$

1.5 (2 pt) Is the solution after the first stage mixed with NaOH excess is a buffer solution? Circle the correct answer: Yes / No.

1.6 (6 pt) Calculate the equilibrium constant for (1) reaction, knowing that the pH of the $0.50\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$ solution is 4.63.

Generated ammonia reacts with boric acid excess. Boric acid is very convenient to use since there is no need to know its exact concentration. After the reaction, the solution can be titrated with a strong acid. In solution, boric acid is ionized by water:

$$\ce{H3BO3 + H2O <=> [H2BO3]- + H3O+} \qquad \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 9.24\ \ (\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} \gg \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2};\ \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a3}).$$

However, studies have shown that boric acid solution contains $\ce{[H4BO4]-}$ ions due to the reaction below:

$$\ce{H3BO3 + 2H2O <=> [H4BO4]- + H3O+}, \qquad \text{reaction } \mathrm{p}K = 9.14.$$

1.7 (10 pt) Assume that both reactions occur in the boric acid solution. Calculate $0.10\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ $\ce{H3BO3}$ pH.

1.8 (7 pt) Draw $\ce{H3O+}$, $\ce{H3BO3}$ and $\ce{[H4BO4]-}$ Lewis structures, including formal charges. Determine central atom geometry (by VSEPR) and write it in the table. [The answer table has a row "Lewis structure" and a row "Geometry (IN CAPITAL LETTERS)" for each of the three species.]

III. Titration and calculations stage

After titration is performed, amount of nitrogen in sample is calculated. To calculate amount of protein, amount of nitrogen is multiplied by specific factor. This factor for milk, rice and meat is 6.38, 5.95 and 6.25, respectively.

1.9 (3 pt) After testing 10.0 g of rice, 19.50 ml of the $1.00\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ HCl solution was used to titrate the final solution. Calculate how much grams of protein is in the rice sample.

Knowing that the protein content is determined by the Kjeldahl method, the Chinese company "Sanlu Group" added melamine to their production for babies. The aim was to increase the amount of protein to be determined. This led to the deaths of 6 children. After investigation, imprisonments and death penalties were assigned for responsible people.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2023-1-fig2.png

1.10 (4 pt) Consider that all nitrogen atoms in melamine are converted to ammonium ions. Calculate how much grams of protein 1.00 grams of melamine imitates in milk, analyzed by Kjeldahl method.

Part I. Manganese – coryphaeus among battery materials

Manganese is predominantly used in making alloys and batteries. Fill in the table to show that novel aqueous Mn-ion battery to compare it to metal-ion and lead-acid batteries from the following considerations. In the case of metal-ion batteries, neglect the electrolytes, respectively; in the case of Pb-acid, account for 35wt% $\ce{H2SO4}$ aqueous electrolyte.

2.1 (13 pt) Calculate the theoretical energy density of the batteries (electrodes and, in the case of Pb-acid battery, also the electrolyte). Assign letters (A–F) denoting advantages and disadvantages (pros & cons) to the corresponding batteries.

A: Electrolyte instability and high cost, low abundance of elements used.
B: Good overall safety, low electrode & electrolyte cost, high abundance of elements used.
C: Robustness, low electrode and electrolyte cost, and wide temperature range.
D: High energy density and good overall performance.
E: Low energy density and environmental issues.
F: Low voltage and moderate energy density.
X: Good safety, high abundance of Mg.
Y: Electrolyte instability and high cost, low energy density and voltage.

$$\begin{array}{l|l|c|c|c} \text{Battery} & \text{Reaction} & \text{EMF (V)} & \text{Theoretical energy density } (\mathrm{Wh\,kg^{-1}}) & \text{Pros} \,\&\, \text{cons} \\ \hline \text{Li-ion battery} & \ce{LiC6 + FePO4 <=> LiFePO4 + 6C} & 3.3 & & \\ \text{Pb-acid battery} & \ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 <=> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O} & 2.1 & & \\ \text{Mn-ion} & \ce{Mn_{0.2}V2O5*H2O + 0.8Mn <=> MnV2O5*H2O} & 1.3 & & \\ \text{Mg-ion} & \ce{2Mg + Mo6S8 <=> Mg2Mo6S8} & 1.1 & 134 & \text{X, Y} \end{array}$$

Part II. Technetium – the lightest of unstable elements

2.2 (17 pt) Fill in the blanks in the text and add missing groups (O, OH, $\ce{H2O}$) to the structures below.

$\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ is one of the most frequently used isotopes in medicinal nuclear imaging. It is prepared in technetium-99m generators as a decay product of 99Mo, obtained in a nuclear reactor in the fission of uranium-235: $^{235}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow \underline{\qquad} + {}^{99}\mathrm{Mo} + {}^{3}\mathrm{n}$. Obtained $\ce{^{99}Mo}$ undergoes _____ decay into meta-stable isomers $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ and $\ce{^{99m2}Tc}$ according to the generic decay diagram (with half-lifes and energy levels).

$\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ undergoes _____ decay of _____ keV comparable to 20–150 keV X-ray range used in conventional radiography. Differently from the latter, detecting the $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ radiation from within the patient's body in a gamma camera gives _____-dimensional images of tissues and organs. The imaging is taken before half of $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ decayed, i.e., within _____ hours after administrating the radiopharmaceutical. $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ radioactivity reduces to 1% of the initial activity in _____ hours. The radioactivity of $\ce{^{99}Tc}$ is __________% of the initial activity of $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$. In most $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ radiopharmaceuticals, $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ (eluted from a technetium-99m generator) is turned into a coordination compound with specific biochemical properties: _______________ attaches to hydroxyapatite and is used to scan bones, _______________ penetrates lipid membranes and is used to scan the heart, _______________ crosses the blood–brain barrier and is used to scan the brain.

With more targeted imaging and therapy, the future applications of $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ for labeling biomolecules will likely be diverse and far-reaching. Technetium _______________ is an essential precursor to specific coordination compounds; it contains two types of ligands – one is a good leaving group, and the other one is strongly bound to technetium.

Part III. Rhenium – an element of supermaterials

Rhenium is used in superalloys and catalysts. Rhenium chlorides are precursors for making catalytic coordination compounds. In reaction with chlorine, rhenium forms solid compound $\mathbf{A}$ ($w_\mathrm{Cl} = 48.77\%$), which thermally decomposes into molecular chloride $\mathbf{B}$ ($w_\mathrm{Cl} = 36.35\%$) and chlorine. Chloride $\mathbf{A}$ is also formed in the decomposition of molecular chloride $\mathbf{C}$, which is unstable at room temperature. The coordination number of Re (including Re–Re bonds) is the same in molecules of $\mathbf{A}$ $[\mathrm{Cl}_a\mathrm{Re}(\mu\text{-}\mathrm{Cl})]_2$, $\mathbf{B}$ $[\mathrm{Cl}_b\mathrm{Re}(\mu\text{-}\mathrm{Cl})]_3$, and $\mathbf{C}$, where μ denotes that chloride is bridging two rhenium atoms (Re–Cl–Re).

Part IV. Bohrium – probably the most boring element in the Universe

Bohrium belongs to the family of superheavy elements, which could act as powerful nuclear fuel, for example, for future fission-propelled space missions. problems.title: Simple Surface Chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Simple Surface Chemistry (18 points, 8% of total)

The surface coverage ($\theta = \dfrac{N_\mathrm{occ}}{N_\mathrm{max}}$, where $N_\mathrm{occ}$ is the number of occupied sites and $N_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum number of adsorption sites) dependence on pressure is described by adsorption isotherms. The most used adsorption isotherm is the Langmuir adsorption isotherm. To derive the Langmuir isotherm, we consider the following rates for adsorption and desorption:

$$r_\mathrm{ad} = k_\mathrm{ad}\,p\,(1-\theta)^{n}$$

$$r_\mathrm{des} = k_\mathrm{des}\,\theta^{n}$$

3.1 (5 pt) Assuming steady state show that the surface coverage $\theta$ dependence on pressure $p$ and adsorption/desorption rate constant ratio ($\alpha = \dfrac{k_\mathrm{ad}}{k_\mathrm{des}}$) takes the form $\theta = \dfrac{(\alpha p)^{1/n}}{1 + (\alpha p)^{1/n}}$.

Further, we will consider a special case – the non-dissociative adsorption – in which first-order rate law is observed for adsorption and desorption ($n = 1$).

In this case, adsorption isotherm is

$$\theta = \frac{\alpha p}{1 + \alpha p}.$$

However, in experiments, we cannot measure occupied sites directly. Instead, we consider the volume of gas adsorbed $V$ versus the volume of gas adsorbed at full coverage $V_\mathrm{max}$, and therefore, the resulting isotherm in terms of volumes is

$$\theta = \frac{V}{V_\mathrm{max}} = \frac{\alpha p}{1 + \alpha p}.$$

With simple algebra, we can linearise the equation to yield that

$$\frac{p}{V} = \frac{1}{\alpha V_\mathrm{max}} + \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{max}}\,p.$$

The following plot was obtained in an experiment of CO adsorption on charcoal at 273 K. Solid dots show experimental data points, and the solid line shows best-fit line.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2023-3-fig1.png

3.2 (4 pt) Using the plot, determine $\alpha$ and $V_\mathrm{max}$.

A useful method to study the kinetics of desorption and determine the desorption activation energy is thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS). In this method, a sample is heated with a linear change in temperature, and the desorption rate is observed. At the temperature where rapid desorption starts, a peak in rate is observed, but after the sample is heated further, the rate decreases due to a lack of adsorbed species. Schematic representation of spectra observed in the studies is shown in figure – multiple peaks represent multiple adsorption sites with their respective desorption activation energies.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2023-3-fig2.png

To extract desorption activation energy $E_\mathrm{d}$, we start from the desorption rate equation and consider that the desorption rate constant follows Arrhenius law, where $\nu$ is the preexponential factor,

$$-\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = k_\mathrm{des}\theta = \nu\theta\exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{d}}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right).$$

Considering that the temperature change during the experiment is $T = T_0 + \beta t$, where $\beta$ is the heating rate, and integrating the rate law, one obtains the relation, where $T_\mathrm{max}$ is the temperature at the top of the peak.

$$\frac{E_\mathrm{d}}{k_\mathrm{B}T_\mathrm{max}^2} = \frac{\nu}{\beta}\exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{d}}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right).$$

3.3 (4 pt) Show that the expression can be rewritten as $E_\mathrm{d} = k_\mathrm{B}T_\mathrm{max}\left(\ln\left(\nu T_\mathrm{max}/\beta\right) - 3.64\right)$. Hint: the quantity $\ln\left(E_\mathrm{d}/k_\mathrm{B}T_\mathrm{max}\right) \approx 3.64$.

TDS experiment was performed to investigate the desorption of ethylbenzene on pyrolytic graphite. Two peaks in the spectra were observed, one at 171 K and one at 209 K. Peak at 209 K corresponds to desorption from the adsorption layer directly on the surface, while the peak at 171 K corresponds to desorption from further layers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2023-3-fig3.png

3.4 (3 pt) Calculate the desorption activation energies (expressed in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) for ethylbenzene desorption from pyrolytic graphite. Assume heating rate $\beta = 1\,\mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$, preexponential factor $\nu = 10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

Hint: the formula from 3.3 provided results in desorption activation energy per atom.

One of the method's shortcomings is that it relies on a good guess of the preexponential factor.

3.5 (2 pt) Calculate the error in the predicted desorption activation energy for desorption at 209 K if the actual preexponential factor is 1000 times larger.
